NEVER A GOOD BARGAIN. —The man who has his price. WHEN is is possible for a secret to come to light? —When it is kept dark. Josu BILLINGS says: " T'ew bring up a child in the way he should go, travel that way yourself." A KANSAS editor has just announced that he will accept anything in payment of subscriptions "except parsnips." SWEET SIXTEEN: "He has such a knightly air !" Seasoned Thirty-five: " Yes ; an up-all- nightly air." TEACHER: "Fritz, tell me the name of the animal who furnishes us with hams?" "The butcher."

"WHAT an air of well-bred repose young New. rich has." " Yes ; but he was naturally lazy to begin with." AWKWARD MISS (with an umbrella) : "Beg par- don." Polite Gentleman: "Don't mention it. I have another eye left." AUNT: "Well, Bobby, what do you want to be when you grow up ? ' Bobby (suffering from parental discipline: "An orphan." "AWKWARDNESS 18 a great misfortune," sighed the nursemaid, as she accidentally dropped the baby down the MEDICAL men are to be envied. If they cure us, we are loud in their praise; if they do not, we preserve a dead silence. How IT STRUCK Him—Terwilliger "What is the worst feature about betting ? " Peterson : " Losing." IN THE SAME BOAT.—Little Clarence: "Pa, is there rea!ly honour among thieves '? " Mr. Calli- pers: "No, my son; thieves are just as bad as other people." AN EXPERT.—WiIIie Slimson : "Papa, how are matches made ? " Slimson : "You'd better ask your mother." "THERE is plenty of room at the top," observed the philosopher who had lost most of his hair; "but there is no use in worrying about it." THE earth goes round, but it would not go round if divided up among all the parties who want it. _ .

ONE source of trouble is that Cupid is apt to discharge his arrows without consulting the girl's parents. UNBEARAELE.—Woman Lawyer: "How old are you?" Woman Witness (trembling) : "Hussy !" LAURA; "I've learned one thing since I got a wheel." Bessie: "What's that?" Laura: "That beauty is only skin deep." HE (after a waltz) : Do you know, I could die waltzing." She (out of breath) : "Perhaps you could, Mr. Hopnot ; but that's no reason why you should expect others to die with you.". MISTRESS (to new servant) : "Your recommen- dations are good, and I think you will do very well. And, now, let me tell you that your mastex is a colonel." Servant: "Oh ! ma'am. I dote on soldiers." HAD TRIED IT.—Hojack : "How did Ethel Tenspot come to marry Mr. Gilgal ? " Mrs. Hojack : "She says she married him to get rid of him." Hojack : "It would have been cheaper for her to have lent him half a sovereign." INSTRUCTION.—Johnny: "And does the gas. meter measure the quantity of gas you use? ' Papa: "No, my son; the quantity you have to pay for." MATE !—lngenious teacher: "If tho clock were to strike fourteen, what time would it be?" Intelligent pupil: "Time to send the clock to be repaired." " BEGORRA," said Pat, with a start, as he opened a bottle of champagne for the first time—" the fool that filled this quart bottle must have put in two quarts instid av wan ! " GRANDPAPA : "Don't get scared, Willie; the tiger is about to be fed—that's what makes him jump and roar so." Willie, easily: "Oh, I ain't afraid of him, grandpa! Papa's the same way when his meals ain't ready !" TIME OF CONTENT.—Dr. Oliver Wendell Holmes once said that when he was young he liked his praise in tea-spoonfuls, that when he got older he preferred it in tablespoons, and alit in advanced years he was content to receive it in ladles. His SAD EXPERIENCE.—" I bought a claim," said the returned Klondiker, "where the nuggets were said to be as plentiful as blackberries." "And they were not?' "Well, yes, they were; but, you see, there were no blackberries in that

region. "DIDN'T you tell that young man I was out?" said the young daughter of tha house. "Oi did, miss," replied Bridget; "but he towld me to come back an' ax yez again, so's to be sure Oi hadn't misunderstood his name." A COUNTRY bookseller, reeeiving.a copy. of an

uncut book, wrote the following to-the ptil3lisher— " I have received the books you sent. One of them is not bound properly. Two of the edges—side and bottom—are left rough and uncut; while the other edge of the leaves—top—is cut and gilded. Shall I take at half-price, or return it ? " GEORGE: "You do not call on Miss Rosebud now" Jack: "No; I got disgusted. She has such a coarse laugh I" George: "I never noticed that." Jack: "You would if you'd been within hearing when I proposed to her." GEORGE: "Do you know what I've a mind to do ?" Bessie: "No." George: "I've a mind to kiss yon." Bessie: "Oh, George, I'm so glad it wasn't true." George: Grad what wasn't true?" Bessie: "Why, Nellie Bassett told me that you hadn't any mind." Bo B.N IN HlM.—Brown: "Bluview is a confirmed pessimist, isn't he ?" Jones: " Yes ; I knew him when he was a boy. One Uhristmas Eve he was as gloomy as an owl because he happened to think how sorry he'd be when Christmas was over."

BY WAY OF REVENGE.—The little fellow was going to a picnic. He jumped out of bed and ran to the window to see what the weather was like. Itr was raining. After gazing out in horror a moment he stamped his foot and exclaimed, "I'll go and worship idols." A GOOD cricket story is told of a certain bishop. He was batting in a local cricket match when the bowler sent a ball very wide of the wicket. "Keep the ball in the parish !" cried the irascible prelate. The next ball sent down knocked the bishop's IPniddle stump out. The bowler shouted—" I think that's somewhere about the diocese, my lud ! " " JouriNv, I find three mistakes on the first page of your letter," said a mother to her nine- year-old son one day. "You have spelled with two l's, 'very' with two r's, and :eft out the word 'brother' in the last line." "I don't call that three mistakes, mamma," replied the boy, calmly, "I call it two mistakes and one forget." "MY FRIEND," he said to one of the convicts, with a patronising air, "never despair. Don't lose heart. No one knows what the future may have in store for you. I was once a poor, miser. able thief like yourself. Now," he added, as he lighted another Havana and threw away the match, "I am a kleptomaniac." OBLIGING.—" Did you say that thil is to be a wedding present?" asked the clever shopman in the china warehouse. "No, I didn't say any- thing of the kind," replied the man who was making the purchase. "And I don' b see that it makes any difference to you." "Not the slightest," was the reply. "I merely thought you might like to have us take off this price mark and paste on another with a higher figure on it." AN aged New York clergyman was going to Brooklyn one Sunday morning to preach. When he reached the pier, the ferry-boat was four or five feet away. In his anxiety he flung first his um- brella aboard, then his satchel, and finally made a tremendous leap himself. But the man who caught him surprised him by shouting, "This boat isn't going out—it's coming L A FUNNY story is Old about a duchess who is very plain, not aristocratic in appearance, and not particular what kind of a gown she wears while out shopping. One day she went into a big shop, where her face was evidently not well known, and seleaed some hem-stitched handkerchiefs, adding, "You may have them embroidered with an X' and a duchess's coronet above." The saleswomen looked in despair at her unattractive customer, and then, in a condescending tone, protested, "Oh, madam, I—l really wouldn't choose a duchess's if I were you !"

div.head: LADIES' LETTER
div.p: LADIES' LETTER

MY DEAR NELLIE, A white crinoline hat will cost a good deal, so I would advise a Tuscan, or a Tuscan-coloured Yedda straw. The shapes turn up a good deal to one side of front, and zuply are trimmed with tulle and mixed roses. Most of the new shapes slope rather over the front. Of three nice hats one is a model in fancy grey straw, with a high crown, and it is trimmed with folds of tucked white chiffon and wing bows of black ribbon velvet, with a fancy open work pattern at the edge. On the left side, under the brim, there is a long black ostrich tip, the stem of which is stuck through the hat, and is seen in the front. There is also a choice paste buckle, which appears to hold the tip in place. I have also seen a very becoming hat of fancy rush straw, with a narrow line of Tuscan straw running through the plait. The brim is lined with tucked mauve chiffon, and tile trimmings consist of large bows of white and mauve satin ribbon and clusters of pink, white, and purple azaleas. Yet another fins confection is of semi-transparent white crinoline straw, with a very high crown, and it is trimmed with light folds of heliotrope tulle and a wreath of _large orchids, shading off from purple to white. 'here is a long paste buckle in frent of the hat.

Fawn sitd silver braid is in great demand for trimming fawn or grey dresses or boleros. The designs are filled in with silver .thread in spider- threads or lattice w07..k, and the most graceful are those which avoid the extreme of elaboration, and yet escape the reproach of meagreness or slovenli- ness. A good effect is made by the choice of colour under these embroideries. For instance, under fawn and gold, or fawn and silver, a little pastel blue silk makes an excellent background, end also makes the fawn colour less trying to the complexion than it otherwise might be. Sallow or over- coloured faces suffer in looks from the proximity unless some telling relief of colour is introduced into the design of the dress or bolero. A tucked gown of beige cloth had a little prawn-pink intro- duced under the embroidery of the vest. The collar was a double frill of pleated muslin with buttonholed edges.

I hear from a very fashionable quarter that boas and ruffles of all kinds are greatly in vogue this spring, and promise to remain so during the sum- mer. Feather boas seem to have taken a fresh Lease of life, the most fashionable variety being either grey or white, rather short, but very full. there is a new tone of " pastel " grey which is particularly in favour. Other stylish boas are made of grey and white chiffon edged with ruch- ings of baby-ribbon, or of spotted lisse, white, on a pink, grey, or black ground. Scarves and ties of yellowish lace are also among the fancies of the season, and range from the wide and long affair that almost takes the place of an outdoor wrap to the simple tie that, knotted sailor-fashion, is worn with a cambric or batiste shirt. Spotted tulle is also largely used for neck-ruffles, as well as for veils and hat-trimmings, although for the latter the fine-meshed cobweb net appears almost more popular. Veils of palest pink tulle with large black velvet spots are novel, but too eccentric to be quite in good taste. Sailor-collars of white muslin and lace are being sold by the hundred at the moment for brightening up -plain silk hk.uses.

Dresses of plain batiste are said to be in pre- paration, but they will not appear till later. Petticoats of this material are flounced and lace- trimmed with almost incredible elaboration, like the silk petticoats, on many of which as much stitching is lavished as once would have been con- sidered far too much for a dre3s. For blouses light colours seem to become more popular with every day. A peculiarly brilliant, rather reddish tone of mauve is one of the latest. There is also a light green which chimes in with the momentary craze for everything that is Irish. Let us hope it may last long enough to give an im- pulse to Irish industries, and draw general atten- tion to them. It was the subject of general comment in Irish circles that until the Queen, had ordered a carpet to be made in Donegal, and the fact was announced in the papers, no one had ever heard that carpets were made in Donegal. People who had lived in that county half their lives were ignorant on the subject. Beautiful specimens oi Irish lace are now exhibited in many shot windows. Your loving JENNIB.

"WOMEN'S CHAT.

Next to Lord Roberts and Baden Powell, General French is one of the most popular heroes of the war, and some interesting details are given of that gallant officer in the • Woman at Home" for June. The family was originally French the same as the came, but afterwards they st tiled in Ireland. From there the Frenches came to England, and tlae General is English by birth, though his mother, who was a Miss Eccles, was a Scotcla- weman. In his early youth: General French seemed more inclined for the pulpit, than for a fighting career. He was the only boy of six ch,ldren, and, as the " man of the family " he appears to have thought that his respon- sibilities lay at home. On leaving school however, he entered the Navy, but not caring for the sea, he changed into the Army. From first to last he has always been an enthusiastic soldier, to what good purpose is manifest in the present war, for no one inspires the Boers with greater terror than General French. His wife was a Miss Selby Lowndes of Bletchley, and General and Mrs. French have three chil- dren, two boys and a girl. One of the boys is at Well- inf4ton College, which the Queen visited the other day. Master French was specially presented t'o Her Majesty, who told him that be must be very proud of his father. _ _ _

Lady Sarah Wilson, of Mafeking fame, is the wife of Captain Gordon Chesney Wilson, .ide-decamp to Major- General Baden-Powell. In her capacity as corresponaent for a London newspaper, she has sent many interesting accounts of the doings in that famous town. Except for a short'time when she was prisoner in Crcnje's camp,Lady Sarhti Wilson has been with her husband throughuut the seige. She possesses a large share of the latent talent and pluck associated with the dueal house of Marlborough, and is quite one of the heroines of Mafeking. Some women it seems have even taken an active part in thP de- fence of the town. There was a Mrs Davies there,a sharp- shooter, who frequently took her plaße in the trenches, and whom it is said, the Boers have good cause to remember. . . _ _

If there is any difference, the burden of a protracted invrstment presses more heavily upon the women than upon the men, but at Mafeking, as at Ladysmith, and Kimberley,they cheerfully bore their shere of the dangers and hardohipa„ and did what was possible to lighten the tedium of,the siege. Sir George White has expressed his admiration for the bravery of the women and girls of Ladysmith, and again at Mafeking.General Baden-Powell has pad a special tribute to the aid rendered ley the women, and the Fplen did fortitude they have displayed throughout the prolonged siege. For the first time, women are to be present at the annual gathering on June 6di of the survivors of the defence of Lucknow. They must, however he relatives of their respective hosts, er have been present in the resithricy during the siege. There are net many women living flaw, who went through that terrible experience. The sieges of Ladysmith, and M .fellinen have been terrible cough, hut they never inwolv,d th. fearful eaesequrnees to the besieged which the fall tn. Luchnow would hiv enrailed. There have unquestionably been some yr:uncle for complaint, hut on the whole the Bosrs appear to have treated their prisonen very well whereas the mutineers in India would base massacred their vic- tims down to the last infant. The many admirers of Madame Antoinette Stirling will be interested to learn that her son, Mr. MacKinlay, has made a successful Cebu- in the concert room. Mac- Kinlay who is a bass, has studied under the veteran Senor Manuel Garcia, who traineJ Jenny Lind, ard Catherine Hayes, and who is now in his ninty-=ixth year. Mr. Maellinlay promises to turn out one of his many successes, and it is understood that Madame Stirling's son intends to adopt concert singing as a pro- fession.

There is a strong belief on the part of many people in Germany, and elsewhere that there is certain to he a cold week in May. This year, these people have not been disappointed far we have had two or three very cold weeks, which shows the wisdom of the old saying "ne'er cast a clout till May be out." The meteorological ex- perts tell us that we may expect a cold summer. Such prognostications about the seasons are little beteer than guesses, but this one is based upon the theory that in the weather, as in most things tbe equilibrium must be maintained. We have had two or three unusually hot summers, and, according to the prophets, we must now expect a cold one to restore the equilibrium. Many milliners will now supply a number of"mounts" with one shape, a delightful arrangement, as in a moment, one mount can be detached and another arranged that matches, or blends with the toilette, with which it is to be weLn. We have long had various coloured binds supplied with each sailor hat, and to- gether with the no w sunshade covers, any number of which can be had with each frame and handle, "quick changes" are within the reach of all. One great disadvantage the long en-tout-cas and sun shade handles undoubtedly possess, is their inadapti- bility to travel. But there are whispers that sticks will shortly appear, which unscrew, and divide into two parts. This will, of course,do away with all discomfort in this direction. The stick fashionable, reaches well above the waist, and the idea makes both for grace and comfort.

In Italy they have an ingenious method of dispersing hailstorms, which not infrequently do great damage to the vines. This is done by means of aerial explosions, for which a special form of cannmn is used, when the threatening hailstones descend in harmless sleet. Some years ago, an Amerisn applied the same principle as a method of producing rain, but repeated experiments proved to be a failure. There is however no question that iti.i a SUOMI for the purpose for which it is used in Italy. The insuring of crops is a very general practice in that country, and the compE.nies greatly reduce their pretnit:ms in those districts which are protscted in this way from hailstorms. Lady Londonderry has just opened the first complete domestic training school which has been erected by the London School Board. it is intended to afford practical training for girls, in all kinds of domestic work, and marks a further stage in the progressive tenth ncy of School Boards. At first the London School Board simply attempted elementary cooking, next laundry work, now we are to have the complete school for household work. There is no doubt much scope for useful work in this direction. though one can hardly help wondering what has become of all the people who always thought that their girls should be taught ordinary household duties at home.

div.head: FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: THE FREE CHURCHES.
DR. MeLAREN IN LONDON.

The famous Manchester preacher has been on a visit to the Metropolis. It is very difficult to get Dr. McLaren to take any outside engage- ments, and many a pastor and senior deacon would like to know how the Baptists at Earls- field managed to get him. Dr. McLaren con- ducted the whole service himself. He looked in good health and his voice rang full and true. He pleaded for the cultivation of the Christian emotions. A representative of the Baptist Times and Freeman tried to interview Dr. McLaren, but it was no good. He said, smilingly, that he had no compassion for inter- viewers. He considers interviewing a noisome pestilence. However, many illustrious men have been interviewed and have lived on to a ripe age, none the worse for it.

div.head: EMPTYING THE PARISH CHURCH!
div.p: EMPTYING THE PARISH CHURCH!

The June Free Church Chronicle contains an interesting sketch of Mr. Carvell Williams, M.P.. the Chairman of the Congregational Union. Mr. Williams is not a stranger to the pulpit. He preached his first sermon at a little chapel in a north Devonshire village. His fame as the champion of Liberation had penetrated even to that remote corner. The result was curious. The squire of the parish, a stiff Churchman, and most of the inhabitants came to listen to Mr. Williams. The parish church was almost empty! Mr. Williams receives occasional visits from both High Church clergymen and Low Church clergymen who are feeling the yoke of the Establishment to be galling and would like to be free from it. He calls these anxious in- quirers his Nicodemuses, and there is an article of furniture in Mr. Williams's room known as the Nicoclemus Chair.

div.head: AUTHOR OF A FAMOUS BIOGRAPHY.
div.p: THE AUTHOR OF A FAMOUS BIOGRAPHY.

The Rev. F. W. Bourne, the well-known minister of the Bible Christian Methodist Con- flexion, is going to retire from active work at the next Conference. Nearly thirty years ago Mr. Bourne published "The King's Son," a memoir of Billy Bray. Billy Bray was a Cornish miner and a local preacher. Without any unusual advertisement, this volume has sold steadily at the rate of a thousand a month from the time of its first publication, and there is no sign as yet of a decreased demand. Alto- gether it has had a circulation of 350,000 copies. Several American papers published it as a serial. It has been translated into several European languages, and into at least one of the dialects of India.
"VOLUNTARY" RATE AND THE QUEEN'S TAXES.

Is it not open to serious doubt whether a collector of Queen's Taxes should be allowed to collect a voluntary rate for the repair of the parish church ? It is estimated that £350 will be needed during the coming year for mainten- ance of the fabric of St. Barnabas Parish Church, Kensington, "its warming and light- ing, and other expenses needful for the decent performance of Divine Worship." The Vestry has been good enough to pass a resolution "that the parishioners submit to a voluntary assessment of 3d. in the £ " to help the church- wardens to raise the money. The rate may be paid to the collector when he calls, or at his offices. Is it right that a Vestry should meddle in a matter of this kind at all? It is only just to add that it is made quite clear on the demand note that the rate is purely voluntary.

div.head: SIMULTANEOUS MISSION, 1901.
div.p: THE SIMULTANEOUS MISSION, 1901.

The National Free Church Council is busy with its preparations for this great effort, which will extend over the whole of England and Wales. We hear that nearly 200 missioners, including the best-known men in the Free Churches, have already consented to take part in the campaign. One hundred thousand copies of the excellent paper read by the Rev. J. Tolefree Parr at the Sheffield meetings are being distributed broadcast. The County and District Federations of Free Church Councils are preparing to do their part well. The Sussex Federation, for example, has appointed a com- mittee to secure missioners for every town and village in the county. Mr. Compton Rickett, M.P., the President, is working with might and main, spending time, thought, and money freely, in the determination to deserve success.

div.head: OLDEST FREE CHURCH IN ENGLAND.
div.p: THE OLDEST FREE CHURCH IN ENGLAND.

A writer in the June Free Churchman claims that the Congregational Chapel at Horning- sham, Wilts, is the oldest Free Church in Eng- land. It bears the date 1566. It was first used for worship by some Scottish workmen who had been brought from over the Border by Sir John Thynne, in order to build a man- sion for him on the Longleat estate. These Scots were strongly imbued wig'. the spirit of John Knox, and with his abhorrease of Popery and Prelacy. Hence the services in the Epis- copal Church did not please them. The article is illustrated with an excellent picture of the quaint old meeting-house which is still used for public worship.

div.head: NEW APPLICATION OF AN OLD PARABLE.
div.p: A NEW APPLICATION OF AN OLD PARABLE.

The Presbyterian missionary meeting is always one of the most successful of the May gatherings in London. This year "lan Maclaren " added distinction to the crowded assembly by his presence in the chair. Many good speeches were made. The raciest was by the Rev. T. T. Matthews, of Madagascar, delivered with a generous Scotch accent and full of Scotch stories. Mr. Matthews, who is in the service of the London Missionary Society, does not relish the presence of the French and the Jesuits in the country. "Of late," he said, "Madagascar has been like the man who wont from Jerusalem to Jericho. You know what happened to him. But there would have been this difference in the case of Mada- gascar : The priests and the Levites did not pass him by. They jumped upon him."

div.head: BISHOP RYLE AND METHODISM.
div.p: BISHOP RYLE AND METHODISM.

The relations between the two Liverpool veterans—Dr. Ryle, who has resigned the Bishopric, and the Rev. Charles Garrett, who is retiring from the head of the Wesleyan Mission—have always been very cordial. When the Bishop first came to Liverpool, Mr. Garrett gave him a personal welcome. In that first interview the Bishop assnred him that, though he was a divine of the Church of England, he was a Methodist, that • his grandfather and father were Methodists, and that he was full of Methodist theology and principles. In fact, the Bishop was proud of, and never tired of, avowing his relationship to Methodism.

div.p: "Lancashire Sketches," &c.
CHAPTER XXVII.

After much weary wandering in various parts of the Transvaal, Stephen Hart returned again to Johannesburg. He could not live peaceably in the outlying districts, for there, despite his resolve to emulate Barnard and be kindly to all men, he found it impossible to live on friendly terms with many of the Dutchmen, who, month by month, became more insulting towarcis Englishmen. At Paardkraal, where he last sojourned, he got him- self into serious trouble by thrashing a burly dopper who had declared in his presence that all Englishmen were cowards. "That's a lie!" said Steve, and to prove it he fell upon the burly Boer unmercifully. For this offence he was hauled up in the Landrost's Court and heavily fined.

- Therefore, when he arrived in the Golden City his views on political affairs in general were some- what different to what they had been twelve months before. Now he was violently anti-Boer. His late experience of Boer prejudices and antipathies had roused within him all his latent pugnacity. "The Boer has become altogether unbearable," he wrote to Barnard. "He is blustering and bombastic, and never loses an opportunity to revile and sneer at Englishmen. He must be thrashed thoroughly, and the sooner our nation commences the thrashing the better." To which observation the kindly consumptive replied: "I have had experience of the blustering Boer you describe, and I have met the other sort, the quiet, inoffensive, hospitable fellow. Such an one is my neighbour, Burman. We never quarrel ;we never talk politics. I help him what little I can, he is very kind to me. If war comes, which God forbid! and I am alive to see it., I3urinan lia,Q asked .me to look to his family. I havr3 promised.' "The Free State Boer is not the Transvaal Boer," :said Steve, as he read his fri?.nd's epistle. "If Barnard lived in this country he would find that there are more blusterers than the other sort." Back in Johannesburg, however, Steve saw little of the objectionable )oer. A few farmers still continued to bring their produce to market, but these men were invariably well-conducted. The Dutch zarps (police) still paraded the streets of the city. Apart from these and a few other individuals, the representatives of the ruling power in the Transvaal were more conspicuous by their absence.

Yet throughout the whole of the city the words "Boer," "Boer Government," "Kruger," "Ooni Paul" were on everyone's lips. Steve passed about from place to place and listened to the views and opinions of everyone. "Between the chains," in Commissioner-street, where the men of stocks and shares daily gathered, he heard the keen fellows discussing excitedly. "I tell you we shall have to fight it out, Sellars. It's no use fooling any longer with Kruger and his crew. Drop negotiations and pick up bullets and drop them in the right place and we'll soon settle matters." _ _

"That's what I say, Nat. Have you signed the petition, Max ? " "Yes, signed it half-a-dozen times. Is that enough? " "Just enough for you, old man. Max is good at that game." "Is he as good at handling a gun as a pen ? " asked Sellars.

"Not so good as you, old man. Here, you'll have to put your fist to this petition, Sellars. "So I will; I'll put both fists to it, and to the Boer's nose as soon as I feel lie oppresses me." "Why, bosh! What's the use of talking like that? We're not oppressed, of course, but we must work some racket up to get this country from the Boers."

"But look here, Sellars," chimed in another, "we pay all the taxes and we get no representation. How's that for square? Call yourself a democrat, too." "Paul would have given the franchise but for that brilliant Raid."

"Would have given us Pretoria, say at once, or would have given us his own hogs head; just as likely. We know those promises of Paul's. Made like his burghers' heads—to be broken. Egad! A lot of those lumbering doppers will get daylight let into their thick skulls soon."
"I say let's fight 'em," said Max. "You fight 'em, d'ye mean, or Tommy Atkins?" "Well, no, i'm not going to have a dust with the dirty burghers. Tommy's willing and ready; let him do it." _ _

"But what does Tommy know of our quarrel? the persistent Sellars asked; "He knows as much as you, b'gad ! I should think. Why are you always sticking up for the Boers, Sellars? Egad II think you're nine-tenths a Dutchman."

"Ten-tenths, you mean," said Nat. "Sellars is a burgher, you know." "Yes, I'm a burgher, and I'm an Englishman. Funny, isn't it? I've been out in this country fifteen years, boys. It's not done bad for me, though it's not been all good. I left Kimberley when the De Beers crowd spoilt it for us fellows, and when I came up to this Johnnys-burg there wasn't a dozen huts here all told. Things were pretty rough, I tell you. But that wasn't all. The niggers kicked up a shindy and I went with the Boer commando to wallop 'em. For that service I got a burgher's vote. So far I'm a burgher. But I'm an Englishman all the same, and that's more than many of you around here are. We've too many ;Jews in this city with English names, but we'll soon see who the right and the wrong ones are when it comes to the scrapping. I tell you I ark, an Englishman bred and born—not made in Germany—and I've an Englishman's love of liberty and fair play, and if I'm oppressed by the Boer, I'm going to fight him. See? I'm not going to stand by and watch Tommy Atkins do it for me. But I'm not oppressed yet, and you're not, and you know it. You know that we've done jolly well out of this country. We've made more of a pile here in five years than we could have made anywhere else in fifty-five, and we're all in that boat, Jew and Gentile, and so long as Paul oppresses us in that style, and let's us have a good pull at his country, I don't mind paying him a bit back for the privilege." Stephen Hart passed on to another group of excited debaters.

"Yes, I'll fight! I'll sign petitions! I'll do anything 1 " cried a man of stentorian voice. "Curse 'em! I'll do anything to alter this state of things. I've lost thousands this last few weeks through this cursed business." "Milner must stiffen his back, and not give way to the old humbug." "That's it, Harker. Milner must stiffen his own back, and break old Paul's." "And his head too, Murray. The old psalm- singing humbug is at the bottom of the whole trouble. Get him out of the way, and we'll soon settle his burghers." "I'm selling out, boys," said Murray. "Who wants to buy a cheap lot ? " Then the group closed in, and excited bargaining began. Everywhere the talk was on the same topic. Johannesburg was in a state of ferment. Would the negotiations now being conducted between the Home Government and the Transvaal Government be productive of any good? "No," was the answer of the Stock Exchange men, the big financiers, and the mine-owners. "War, and war alone will remedy our grievances. The Boer Government must be overthrown, and British rule be substituted."

And through all the turmoil and heat of discus- sion of political questions, the voice of one little assembly was nightly heard in the market-place of the Golden City preaching peace, and calling upon all, Outlander and Boer, Jew and Gentile, to seek salvation and the Kingdom of God. Once or twice Stephen Hart, weary of discussing the eternal political theme, had turned towards this little group of Salvationists, and listened to their service.

On a certain Saturday night in May he was thus standing on the fringe of the crowd which gathered round the "Army," when a trio of drunken fellows lurched across the market-place, and burst noisily into the ring. "Make room for three recruits, Cap'n," bawled the leader, stumbling forward. . _ _ .

"Right, brother ; we're glad to see you," the Captain cheerily answered, perceiving the condition of the noisy fellows, yet in his large tolerance, so characteristic of his people, making allowances. "But when you join God's army, my lad, you must become a sober recruit." _ _

"Aye, yes, that's so. We'll come sober nex' time, eh, boys ?'" His two companions grunted assent. “Sing on, cap'n ; we'll join in." The tune so rudely linterrupted was continued, the Salvation lasses tapping their tambourines and a coloured girl strumming a banjo accompaniment. Stephen Hart pushed his way through the crowd until he got near to the inner circle, directly oppo- site the three topers, who were now noisily bawling the song. The man who had first spoken stood in front of his two comrades, and, as he raised his head and the lamp-light fell upon his face, Steve recognised Ralph Cartleigh. The song ended Cartleigh stepped forward a pace and peered keenly into the faces of the women assembled about him. _ _
"Ah, all white faces but one, and mostly good- looking, cap'n,. 'specially that one." The young woman indicated shrunk bark into the shadow of the lamp and drew her poke bonnet closer about her face.

"If all your soldiers were as pretty as that one, cap'n, I'djoin your regiment at once. But, no, I wouldn't I Curse your pretty faces! I shouldn't have been standing here now if it hadn't been for a pretty face. I followed it seven thousand miles— that pretty face—then the jade jilted me. Curse, her! I've had nothing to do with your women since, and never will have more!" He fell back on his hiccoughing companions, who tried to draw him away. ."Come on, Percy; .this ain't no place for you. It's not the Salvation Army you want, it's the other." am.

"Yes, that's me, cap'n. I'm Fighting Percy, I We're going to have some fine battles in this country soon and I'm going to be in at the scrapping." "Fight on the Lord's side, my lad, then we'll perhaps avoid the other war." "Join your army, eh ? " said Cartleigh, coming back into the ring again. "Gad! I will, cap'n, if you'll take out that ugly nigger's face from your ranks. It doesn't go well alongside that pretty white one."
"S-s-sh 1 Don't say that, brother. Black and white are both alike to God."

The drunken fellow was roused to sudden wrath by this remark. "White and black aren't both alike to me. Niggers are devils, every one of 'em. They've no souls to save. Take that ugly face out of your crowd or I'll knock it out!"

"Sister, come here," s said the captain to the frightened Hottentot. The little woman stepped forward a pace, when Cartleigh rushed towards her and struck out viciously. But the blow missed her, for the young woman with the fair, white face stepped between and received it full on her cheek. She dropped to the ground instantly. _
"You co-i-vard !"

Stephen Hart's fist shot out like a piston-rod, and when he drew it back Ralph Cartleigh was sprawled at his feet. The little band of Salvationists hurried away with Sister Ella as a noisy crowd gathered round antici- pating a fight. "Get up, Percy, and give him beans," said one of Cartleigh's associates. "Give him peas—l mean peace," said a man in the crowd. "Percy wants peace and rest after that knock-out blow."

Such appeared to be the case, for Fighting Percy seemed in no humour for combat. He lay back in the arms of his companions mild stared stupidly at the stalwart fellow who had just floored him. Presently he stumbled to his feet and lurched forward a pace, and, as Steve put himself in a defensive attitude, the crowd expectantly waited the attack.
But Cartleigh, having made sure of his man, retreated. .
"Fight that miserable creature ? " he sneered. "Not I. I've fought him this last two years in another game and I've, beaten him, and he knows it. See! See how he shews it!"
Steve's face was ashen pale. With difficulty he restrained himself from striking his taunting enemy. _ _ _

"I've beaten him all along-the line. I-took ids girl from him. Then she beat me. She gave me the slip. She has beaten us both. Steve the Out- lander, we are quits." Saying this Cartleigh turßed his back on his antegonist and pushed his way through the crowd. "Fight it out! Fight it out!" yelled the bystanders. "Not to-night, I'm not sober enough. We'll settle it before long, then one of us shall go down for ever," and Fighting Percy quickly vanished in the darkness, leaving Steve alone troubled by dis- turbing reflections. "Ella has beaten us both," he said. "What could he mean? Followed her seven thousand miles, then she gave him the slip. Did she repent after writing that terrible letter? Did she regret? Ah, well, it matters not, we are parted now for ever. All that remains now is for Cartleigh and me to settle our account with each other. The sooner the better."

div.head: CHAPTER XXVIII.
div.p: CHAPTER XXVIII.
obannesburg was at fever heat. The negotiations between the 13ritish and the Transvaal Govern- ments had failed of their object and war was inevitable.

War, in all its bloody horror; war, which would cast dire desolation and misery throughout this erstwhile prosperous land; war, which would smear this land of gold deep red with the blood of gallant men; war, which would water the trampled wastes with the tears of women and children; war, inexorable, evil-righting, passion-allaying, terrible, glorious war I "Yes, a glorious war 'twill be," said the fat financiers of the Golden City, as they prepared to depart from the scene of the future conflict to make more room for Private Tommy Atkins. "A glorious war 'twill be," said the peaceful, pushful Jews, as they hurriedly gathered up the shekels and crossed over the border of the ill-fated Transvaal.
"A glorious war 'twill be," yelled the noisy horde of howlers who had long "fought Kruger with their mouths," as they skipped into sunny Natal.

"A glorious, righteous war 'twill be," said the Outlanders, as they joined the Imperial Light Horse and prepared to tack up their opinions with eloquent action. "A grand, glorious war 'twill be," said other Outlanders, joining the Irish-Americans, the Germans, and the Hollanders, and forming corps to fight with the Boer commandos as allies. "A justifiable war it will be," said Stephen Hart, as he attached himself to the Imperial Light Horse and prepared to depart to Ladysmith. Combatants and non-combatants all looked eagerly forward to the fray. It would settle Outlander grievances, it would eliminate race-hatred, it would once and for all firmly establish British supremacy throughout South Africa.
All were agreed that it would be "a glorious war."

In the 'Frisco bar, in Eloff-street, a cosmopoli- tan crowd of nondescripts assembled nightly, as they had done for months past, to discuss the situation. On October 2nd Fighting Percy—as Ralph Cartleigh was designated by the frequenters of the canteen—was holding forth on the all- absorbing theme. His audience was composed of representatives of all nationalities, but the Irish-American element predominated. Most of the men were drunk, and frequently interrupted the speaker with noisy remarks. Mingling with the crowd was a tall, military- looking man, quiet and unobtrusive, yet ever watchful and alert.

This man was a Transvaal Secret Service official. For years he had, under various disguises, mingled with all classes of society in the disaffected city, and much valuable information had he gathered for his employers during this period. To-night, as he listened to Fighting Percy's somewhat discursive remarks, he carefully noted their effect on the auditors, particularly observing each man who applauded certain of the speaker's sentiments. "Yes, I'm a curious sort of a human mixture, I am," said Cartleigh, in answer to a question from one of the audience. "As curious a mixture as most of you fellows around here. You ask what countryman I am, sonny. Well, when I'm drunk I'm a Britisher, when I'm sober I'm a Boer, when I'm half-and-half I'm a howling Outlander. Bee ?"

_ "Bully for Percy! Here's to Fightin' Percy I " yelled the men. "Yes, that's me, boys. When you see me in any of those three states, you'll know what label to stick on me. Fill me well, and fill me tight, and for England, home, and beauty, I'll fight. "An' which side are ye goin' to bight on, Percy ? " asked an Irish-American. "When the fighting comes on, I shall be a sober Boer, my boy, and I only hope I shall have half a chance to bore a hole through some of the absent Jew-Anna's beggars who have helped to kick up this shindy. Look at 'em. boys

IJOOK at these .1 - Anna's beggars, I:l°vr they've been snuffling and snivelling betweell the chains, these last few weeks, wondering how much compensation they'll get from our BrittY Government after the row's over. Oh, I'd give 'em compensatim, boys I'd fill 'em full of it; but not in gold—no, lead, boys. Yes, of all the men in this Jewhannesburg that I'd like to meet when the scrapping begins, the Jew is foremost; after him, the rest of the howling crowd who ha" been mouthing it.so bravely about their grievance° up here. But I reckon we shall miss these absellt: 11 minded beggars when the fighting begins. They go down to Capetown and Durban, and shout hall for Tommy Atkins to come across the water an ° fight for 'em." "You're pretty rough on 'em, Percy," said a man at Cartleigh's elbow. ,a "Yes, and I'd be rougher on 'em later if thekg, give me the chance; but no fear, there'll hot many Jew Jew financiers fighting on either side. We Britishers will be fighting each other, and it'll be?' stiff business, you'll see. And after the row 115 over, these financial vultures, Jews and Gentiles, will swoop in here again, and reap all the benefit' Curse -'ern I " "You're getting too Boerish, Percy. Fill up glass, and make him more of a Britisher. rereY'a too sober to-night." The glass was filled and re-filled, and soon Cart" leigh was quite intoxicated. "Now," he hiccoughed, tilting his hat over hi! ear and assuming a sparring attitude, "where's tu man that called me a Boer? Where's the we° that wants to fight a Britisher? Fetch your burghers along; we'll wallop 'em! We'll teac' your ignorant doppers how to rule and how to fight. We'll shew 'em that Englishmen are Englishmen all the world over, and aren't going to be bossed and bullied by anyone, least of all by Kruger end, his sanctimonious Boers. Who says Majuba Fetch your burghers along; we'll give 'eral Majuba! Three cheers for Joe Chamberlain' Hooray Hooray Hooray! CBoos I ' and howl° of execration from the Irish-Americans.) Three cheers for Milner, and groans for Oom Paul Hooray! Hoo—" Here the speaker was interrupted by a flyieg bottle, which struck his head and bowled him over. The rest of Fighting Percy's martial speech W 55 spoken incoherently as he lay doubled up on th° floor. Finally he fell asleep in this uncomfortable posture, and when he was roughly awakened two hours later the canteen was being cleared of iti° noisy occupants. He reeled out of the place, all' the fresh night breeze, fanning his flushed facet refreshed and sobered him.

"Ralph Cartleigh !" said a voice in his ear' whispering low. "Yes, what is it ? " he said, turning in alarm, *$ his old, half-forgotten name was spoken. The Secret Service man confronted him. "You made a promise to Jan Schultz nine monthg ago ? " "I did, and—l will keep it." "Follow me 1" said the official, and silently thei passed through the deserted streets, followed 1)1* group of the *Frisco bar habituics. (To be continued.)

glad that they were distributing it. He uuld assure them that he did not begrude one penny of it. (Hear, hear.) This year they had made a change and he wanted everyone to understand why they had made it. Previously each man hal r celved half his bonus in shares arid half in c.s.r. The found:Aim and real root of this profit sharing busi rise,s was to endeavour to teach and help the moo to begin to save. Last year the half bonus paid in cash was deposited for the men in t. e Warrineton Savings Bank. A sum of about £3lO was pail into the batik and within two days something like £290 of it was with- drawn. (Laughter.) He did not go so far as to say that the money was not spent wisely ; he would give them all credit for having spent it in the best direction. But ke was anxious that they r,hould begia save, and he thought that a man who earned more than thirty shillings a week ought to save at least a ve-ek's wages in a year. Under the profit sharing scheme a man who had earned £2 a week right throulh the year weolii gr.'s; a bones of £5; and one who had earned £75 would get £3 lbs. It was not a gie st d -al bit what he wanted to arrive at was this, was th:ne; any man present who fowl been maltinc thirty shillings a week who had saved £3 15s. in the year? A WORKMAN : We have families to keep.

Mr. Melillo/en said he knew that their families pre- vented many from saving. But if they wer- not saving a week's wages, Richmonde by their pr_ fit sharing sehetne were thing more for them than they were doing ler themselves. (Applause). In response to an invitation of Mr. RICHMOND, it Was ascertained by a show of hands that there were only twelve out ef over 400 workmerepreseut who had saved £2 in the year. (Laughter). Mr. RICHMOND (continuing) said it was all right to laugh about it now, but if sickness came, and old age crept on they would probably wish that they had saved a little. (Hear, hear.) He wished them to begin to save. By drawing the bonus money out of the Savings' Bank they were not saving, and therefore in the men's own interests the firm had decided to distribute he bulk of of the bonus in shares, so that it could not be spent. These shares would immediately earn interest at the rate of six per cent. and in a short time would accumulate to such an extent that the interest would be as large as the bonus. It was enly a little at the beginning, but, as the Scotchman would say "every mickle makes a mu .I.eaa:' (Laugh- ter) Then were some people who would not begin to save because they could not save a lot, but they would never save a lot until they began with a little. (Hear, hear) The firm were tre jug to make their workpeople feel that they should make provision for themselves who's they were unable to follow their employment and were doing their best te help them to take this step in the right direction. They had an interesting feature at Strat- ford when he (Mr. Richmond) distributed the profits a short time ago in the fact that they had one of their work- men present who bad been wounded at Peardeborg. He wascOne of the men who left their Stratfordlworks to obey his country's call.and there were two others from Strat- ford wise were still at the front. From the Warrioreten works they had parted with a dozen moil who were on ac- tive service in South Africa,and,oF that number,fiye of them were profit sharers. They bad more men at tile frost than any ether firne,in Warringtoniand he was clad that it wasa characteristic of Richmonds to be always at the front. (sear, hear and laughter.) He hoped their men at the front weuld make their presence felt. He wanted those present to give them, in recoenition ofithe relief of Mafeking, three rousing British cheers. Three cheers were then given with enthusiasm, and Mr. Richmond asked the friends of the men at the front to tell thorn how their names were received. These men he said, who go to fight for tbe honour of our country and the glory of our Queen ought not to be forgotten, and they would see to it that their wives and chi Pren were looked after whilst they were away. Proceeding to refer to the annual excursion,he said he was glad that they had made a chaege,and were going to Douglas this year instead oi Blackpool. The " Qsoei Victoria "or "Prince of Wales" had been chartered for the trio, and either vessel was capable of accemmodating 1,500. He only hoped they would have a smooth passage,anel that nene of them would have cause to be sorry whilst crossing the Irish Sea. (Laughter.) He had one word more to say. In the envelopestwhich he was about to present to them they would find their share certificates and the interest due to them. As they left the building they would lied a representative from the Post Office, in the lodge, who would be pleased to open a bankieg account for them, and take from them any of the spare money they found in the envelopes. They would see that the firm were doing all they could for them and be wou'd ask them pereonally not to let all this work be wasted. Mr Hughes Mr Davy, and Mr Ransome had ?taken a great deal of trouble in this matter and he did not want them to feel that the labour was in vain. (Applause.) Mr. J. A. RANSOMS, who had a cordial reception, said that was the first time he had had the pleasure of addressing them officially. It gave him greet pleasure to witness the profit, sharing distribution. There were at least twe ocoasions in the year when they had the opportunity and pleasure of seeing Mr. Richmond, and these were the profit-sharing distribution and the annual excursion. Mr. Richmond, as they were aware, was a busy man and almost wanted to crowd a week into a day. (Laughter.) Mention had been merle of the in- creased prosperity of the firm and to the fact that toey were always at the front. He wished to impress noon them that it depended upon each one —from the smallse boy in the works to the leading official—whether they were to maintain their present positioe. (Hear, htar ) If everyone did his very best in his own department there would be more profits aud; larger bonuseo for everyone. (Applause.) Mr. HUGHES said he had pleasure in propo;ineZa vote of thanks to Mr. Richmond. They were in- debted to bim not only for his presence that dry but also for introducing theprofit-sharing scheme. (Hear,hear.) It was due to Mr. Richmond's personal effort and generous disposition that the scheme wee inaugurated, and, hr fore it cold be introducel, Mr. Richmond had to rerseede a good many of the directorate and leading officials, to give it a trial. He remembered Mr. Richmond saying that he would give it a five years' trial. Personally, he (Mr. Hughes) •hao tnot much faithlin the sehemeott the beginning ; but,now, he believed it would grow to ho a very esooi thing for all concerned. They could best show their gratitude to Mr. Richmond by each one, doing his duty even ore earnestly and more faithfully than ever before. (Applause.) Mr. DAVY briefly secended the proposition which was earned with acclamation. Mr. RICHMOND in acknowledging the compliment, stated that he had omitted to mention that a resolution had tem agreed to by the Profit Sharing Committee fig- bag the selling price of these £1 six per cent preference shares which were being distributed as bonuses. In the event of these preference shares being required at any time ttiroueh the reconstruction or Amalgamation of the Company, it had been decided that the price at which they could be booght was not to exceed 28 dell- lings per £1 share. ( lonlause-) On the suggestion of Mr. RICHMOND it was decided to send their best wishes to Mr. Harold Reneome and ex- press the hope that he would soon be fully restored to health. (Cheers). Mr. J. A. RANSOME said he was pleased to say that his brother was getting better. (Applause.) Mr. RICHMOND then made the oistribution and the interesting proceedings terminated.

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY, MAY 25, 1900.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, MAY 25, 1900.

opposing them in the Town Hall Ward for some time to come. (Hear, hear.) The contest hal been conducted in an amicable manner, and the result of the excellent work which had been dine was that he had been re- turned by a majority of 265. H could only say hat now he was a member of the Council he should do his best in the interests of all the ratepayers and the town generally. (Applause.) He must again thank them for the splendid and hard work they had done that day. Councillor SMETHURST (chairman of the Ward Com- tnittee) said they had had a very hard day's work but they had gained a glorious victory—a victory which, he hoped, would serve as a warning to their friends such as Mr. Dixon, who had only polled 20 votes. (Laughter.) He believed no contest would have taken plaee but for his nomination. However, there had been an election, , and Mr. Forshaw had won by 265 votes. He had said that some hard work had bees done, and willingly done. There had been a few backsliders. Some whom they had expected to work had not done so, but they would for- give them and trust they would be good friends. The present, in his opinion, was one of the most glorious victories they had ever won in the Town Hall Ward, and he was personally very much obliged to those who had put their shoulders to the wheel. It was pleasing to know that their labours had not been' in vain. The re- sult was very gratifying. Councillor FORSHAW said he had omitted to state that the Conservative party had a splendid agent in Mr Hol- brook, whose organisation was perfect. (Hear, hear.) He had worked hard that day, and his (the speaker's) thanks were also due to the members of tlae Junior Con- servative Associati in. (Applause.) Alderman SUTTON said it was with much pleasure he congratulated Mr. and Mrs Forshaw upon the great success which had been obtained that day. Much praise was due to Mrs Forshaw for the manner in which she had worked in bringing uo voters to the poll. Mr Forshaw ought to be proud of such a valuable wife. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He had heard many people say they had never seen a lady work so bard. He had been connected with many muni— cipal contests in Warrington, but he had never seen greater zeal on the part of the workers than had been manifested on that occasion. If the Conservatives would only put their shoulders to the wheel thy never need fear an election. Some good work had been done by the members of the Junior Conservative Association,and ke hoped it would encourage them to assist that club. (Hear, hear.) Some people objected to the present arrangement—the compromise—and maintained that the voters were in a measure disfranchised by it, but he thought from the experience they had already obtained, they would agree that it had been a difficult matter to And a good candidate otherwise. He m,ant a man who possessed influence in the town and was a large rate- payer. It had been impossible, hitherto to induce such men to come forward. He contended that the present arrangement was a benefit to the ratepayers, and that it had men carried out very fairly by both political parties. (Hear, hear.) The Liberals by their agent and by their workers had tried to do their best to keep the compact between them and had helped them to return their candidate. Under those circumstances he thought the compromise a very satisfactory one. (lElear,hear.) Councillor SHILLCOCK said he would like tte add this testimony to the gentlemanly manner in which the con- test had been conducted. No one more heartily con gratulated Mr. Forsbaw than he did, and if it should ever be his (the speaker's) lot to contest the Town Hall Ward again, he hoped it would be his good fortune to have Mrs. Forshaw on his side. (Laughter and applause.) She no doubt felt proud that her efforts had been crowned with such success. He hoped that the compact to which reference had been made would be continued for some time, because owing to the great changes in the municipal government of Warrington it was only right that those who now held the strings should be enabled to carry out such great improve- ments as electric lighting, the introduction of tramways, street widening, and extension of the sanitary system, which involved an expenditure of nearly £300,000 (Applause.) It was only right that those men who had taken part in the initiatory stage of the work should be allowed to carry it to a successful issue. (Applause.) Warrington in the near future would be pieced in the front van of municipal Government. Before the year was over it would become a county borough, and they would have the management of the whole aff sirs of the town in their hands.

Councillor JOHN ROBERTS also spoke, and alluded to the hard work which had been done by Mrs. Forshaw. She was, he said, the champiln, and not her husband, who ought to feel proud of the pluck she had displayed. The contest had been fought in an honourable manner, and they were all pl>ased with the large majority of votes which Mr. Forshaw had received. He wai bound to confess that their Liberal friends had acted loyally with regard to the compact,and he trusted that it would lest for some considerable time. (Hear, hear.) He had been very pleased to see many of their opponents taking such an interest in the Conservative candidate and help- ing to return him. They ought to be very thankful to the Liberals, and he thought it would be their duty to return the compliment at some future time. (Hear. hear).
Three hearty cheers were then given for Mr. Forshaw.

div.head: FOOTBALL CLUB MEETING. Election-(7-Officers.
div.p: FOOTBALL CLUB MEETING. Election-(7-Officers.

There was a very satisfactory attendance at the annual general meeting of the Warrington Football Club held on Thursday last week in the Workman's Club. Market Place. Mr. T. Bowers occupied the chair in the absence of the President, and amongst those present were Mr H Ashton (hon. secretary), Mr. T Pemberton (hon. treasurer), Mr r Wallington And Mr. W. Webiter (auditors), Messrs T Birnes, sen., W Hewitt, W Nevins, F H rimer, W Hill, J Hackett, T Barnes, jun.' S Wright, E V Walker, Freeman, Shaw, T Hill, L Bate, W Taylor, F Longshaw, J T Bate J T Thorniley Job Jones, A Titchett, Burdett,and E Roberts. The President.

On the proposition of Mr. THOMAS WALLINGTON, Mr. T. Bowers was voted to the chair: Tie CHAIRMAN thanked the members for electing him to that plsition and explained that the president of the club had unfortunately been obliged to go on a long tour for the benefit of his health. The boat on which he was travAling was not due in this country until the 27th Inst. They would therefore have to manage without his services at that meeting.

div.head: Reports.
div.p: The Reports.
The repots and statement of accminta hr the past season which have been already printed in the "Examiner" were taken as read. The CHAIRMAN invited discussion on them.

Mr. FRANK El iTuntiEn called attention to the expenses in connection with the Warrington Junior League and asked the Secretary whether he could give any explana- tion of the item "Myself £3 18s 2d." The SECRETARY said it was a little error which had crept into the account and he was glad of that oppor- tunity of explaining it. In the early part of the season he was requested by the committee to ask the treasurer of the Junior League for a statement of accounts. He learneci that it had been disbanded and with the object of getting information the committee instructed him to ask for the reason why it had been broken up. The item of £3 18s 21 under the heading of" myself" referred to the treasurer of the Junior League. He had written for an explanation on more than one occasion but the only statement that could be got from him was that he felt that he was entitled to that amount for his services to the junior league. (Laughter.l Mr. FREEMAN proposed the adoption of the report and balance sheet.
Mr. FRANK TURNER seconded and said he was glad he had agked for the explanation as it threw all blame off Mr. Ashton.

div.head: Tao pr,p )sition was unanimously carried. Honorarium to the Hon. Secretary and Treasurer.
div.p: Tao pr,p )sition was unanimously carried. Honorarium to the Hon. Secretary and Treasurer.

Mr F. H. TURNER in proposing a resolution" That the sum of £25 each be voted to the lion: secretary and hon. treasurer as an honorarium for their services during the past year,"said be was sure they might congratulate the officers of tha club on the very effi .dent way tney had conducted the business during the past season. Their friend and treasurer,Mr. Pemberton had been with them a glee, many years and bad earned their r spect anci appreciation for the way he had carried out his onerous duties. (Hear, hear.) Speaking as the representative of the Lancashire and Ceeshire Referee Society and as one who had many opportunities of observ- ing the m*thode adopted by various clubs in financial matters he had no hesitation in saying that he believed their system at Warrington was in front of any other in the Northern Union. (Ap piause). Their method at WaTrington of checking the gate money was superior to any other. Their treasurer was assisted') by a staff which was a credit to them- selves and the club. (Hear, hear.) It was generally admitted that the treasurer to the Warrington Club was one of the finest business men in the Northern Union, and he (Mr. Turner) hoped they would retain, Mr. Pemberton for many years to come. With reference to their friend, Mr. Ashton, he thought they could congratulate him upoa the splendid manner he had discharged his duties during his first year of office as secretary. (11 iar, hear.) He had worked efficiently and untiringly to maintain and uphold the honour of the club. Mr. Ashton had the beat interests of the club at heart, and had come through the ordeal in a most successful manner. He had therefore great pleasure in moving the resolution. (Applause.) Mr. T. BARNES, jun., seconded and the resolution was unanimoe sly carried,

div.head: Auditors.
div.p: The Auditors.

Mr. F. H. TURNER then proposed that the auditors be allowed the sum of £5 each for their services during the past year. He referred to the great amount of time which was given by the auditors on Saturday afternoons ia checking the receipts and to the labour involved in auditing the acclunts. He thought they were entitled to the honorarium which he now proposed. (Hear, hear.) M. HACKETT secluded. _ _
Tk C—h-a—ia--11-A-N---said---he was sure the auditors bad earned it.—rtoey devoted a great deal of time to their duties.
The resolution was unanimously adopte Re-election of Officers.

On the propos tion of the CHAIRMAN, the following offilers care unanimously re-elected ; President, Mr Ernest L Fletcher ; Hm. Treasurer, Mr T Pemberton ; Hon. Secretary, Mr H Ashton ; Hon. Auditors, Messrs T Waliipgton, ani W Webster. The Committee Thanked.
Mr. T. WALLINGTON proposed a vote of thanks to the committee f9r their valuable work durinc; the past year and referred in felicitous terms to the excellent work which had been done.

Mr. BATE seconded and the meeting unanimously agreed: 'file CHAIRMAN, in responding said all the members of the comauttee had done their best for the interest of the club. It was not all " sunshine." There was a -great deal of work to be thne but if they had an intereit and a love for it they did not think much of the labour. He was pleased to say they had a very good committee; in fact, it had been one of the pleasantest he had ex- perienced during his connection with the Warrington Football Club. It would perhaps have beaa note,' that the elcction of captain, sub-captain and touch judges had aot been left with the annual meeting this year. The reason was that the members of the team were all paid players and it was only right that the committee should have the power to elec', the captain or sub- captain. If the meeting elected a captain, for some reason or other he might not play awl the team would then he without a captain. The committee desired t elect a playing captain for the sewn. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: Ballot for the Committee.
div.p: Ballot for the Committee.

Voting papers were distributed for the election of a committee. Nine persons were nominated for the six vacant seats. Messrs Webster, Burdett, Freeman, Hackett,Thomas Hill and Samuel,Wright were appointed tellers. The result of the ballot -gas that the retiring committee was re-elected, viz : Messrs T Barnes, sea.. T Sewers, W Dillon, W Hewitt, W Nevins, and J T Thorniley. Mr. P. BARNES, senior in thanking the meeting for re-electing him on the committee said that fast year he was a st,rn critic of the proceeiinge bat he was not so at the present time. (Laughter.) He ceuld say this,that the committee had worked harmoniously together during the pa-it season. (Hear, hear.) He had beard remarks in the pest that it had been composed of cliques and that there had been constant friction but he could assure them that hed not been the case with the commi,tee which had just been re-elected for another year. The work during the past season was of a very arduous ch,tracter and i: was only those who bad been eugagei in it who fully appreciated the amount of work which had fallen upon the ,heulders of the emell committee. He thought they had considerably improved from a playing poiut of view. (Bear, hear.) Such an exposition as was given by their team in the latter part of the season was in every way worthy of any team in Enelaed. (Flear,hear.) They were going to commence th-i next seeeion with men who were first rate players. He was pleased to say that there was a better understanding amongst them and if the weather was favourable, for that had much to do with their combination, he thought the result next year would be evou better than the past (Applause.) They 'lee not had the pleasure of having the assistance of their President on many cceasions. but he remembn.ed that on one occasion when a matter was brought forward of great importance with regard to improving the management of the club. their President said they must have business before pleasure, and that had been the Committee's motto &icing the past year. He could assure *zhem that nothing should be wanting on hio part as a member of the Committee to improve the position of the club. (Applause).
