div.head: Trustees.
div.p: Trustees.
Mr. PEMBERTM proposed that Mr. B)wers and Mr. Borroa the retiring trustees be re-elected. Mr. WEBSTER seconded and the resolution was unanim- ously carried.

div.head: Thanks to the Press.
div.p: Thanks to the Press.

Mr. T. BARNES said that greater publicity, was being given to their football matches and he was sure that the excellent reports and sometimes the scathing criticism that the tenni had to submit to were beneficial. It helped them to form abetter opinion of the team they had at Warrington and to give attention to defects. He thought the members would agree with him that the best thank ought to be given to the press for their services. (Hear, hear.) Mr Salm seconded the resolution which was unanim- ously carried. Mr F FENNELLY briefly returned thanks for the Press. The Chairman:

Mr PEMBERTON proposed that the best thanks of the meeting be given to the Chairman for his services. From the list of attendances they would see that Mr Bowers had not put in quite the number of attendances thatihe had done in the previous year, but that had not been hi fault. He bad been confined to the house through ithors but his interests were always for the best welfare of the club. His services were valuable to the club in many ways. Mr. E. V. WALKER suggested that before the motion was put it would be as well to pass a vote of condolence with the President of the club (Mr. E. L. Fletcher) in the loss he had sustained by the leath of his mother. Mr. PRANK TURNER seconded this proposition and said be was sure that every member of the club sympa- thised with Mr. Fletcher. The resolution was carried. Mr. BATE then seconded the vote of thanks to the Chairman which was unanimously carried. In acknowledging the complimant the CHAIRMAN said he was more of a worker than a speaker, but be could promise them that he would do all that lay in his power to keep the club going. He had been a member of the committee for a number of years but the past season had been one of the pleasantest he had ever experienced. Previously they had been troubled with a very large committee and thought an improvement had been effected in reducing the number. Matters had been thoroughly thrashed out and the business had been con- duced in a syt3rnatic way. With the present state of affairs in football circles the work had to be carried on in a business way if they were to come before the mem- bers with a satisfactory balance sheet. (Applause.) This concluded the meeting.

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTION AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: MUNICIPAL ELECTION AT WARRINGTON.
Mr. Forshaw Returned.

Three candidates entered the contest in Town Hall Ward on Monday for a seat on the Warrington Town Council. In accordance with the agreement between the two political parties the election was not fought on political grounds. The Conservatives were entitled to return a member under the com- pact and accordingly they brought forward a strong cautiidate in the person of Mr. Forshaw. solicitor. The Master Butchers' Association being anxious to have a representative on the Council in view of the decision to erect a public abattoir in the town, de- cided to bring forward Mr. Henry Singleton. At a later stage Mr. F. Dixon,metal merchant of Parker- street, entered the fray on behalf of the Property Owners and Ratepayers' Association, but be did not conduct the contest with any earnestness and his opposition was not taken seriously. Soma years ago Mr. Dixon was a member of the Council. In his ad 'rem he informed the electors that he had had "many years' municipal experience." He stAtd that he is "strongly opposed to the disfranchising of tree ratepayers by arrangement between the two political clubs. He is free from all personal or ' party ties, and pledges himself to act solely in the interests of the ratepayers." A. circular was issuHd by Mr. John Crosfield (president of the Warringtoa Liberal Association) an 1 Mr. John White (chairman of the Warriugton Conservative Asso- ciation), on behalf of Mr. W. I. Forshaw. Toe circular Informed the voters of the ward,who number 1032,that the Lib-ral and Conservative Associations entered into an agreement for the purpose of rendering unnecessary any political contests in municipal elections for a period of two years, and in a circular to the voters they said : The objects which the leaders of the political parties have haa, are twofold, viz., to prevent the serious expenditure of tbe ratepayers' money which these contests entail, and to fill such vacancies as may occur from time to time in the representation of the various wards by the election of capable men more or less largely interested in our Leanufacturing industries the development and extension of which are so vital to the future prosperity of the community. As previously intimated, the work of the municipal year upon which we have entered promises to be of a very arduous and important character, and if the various undertakings which the Corporation already have in hand are to be carried to a successful issue, it is absolutely essential that those men, and those only, whose personal , capacity, wide experience, and personal integrity can be implicitly relied upon, should be elected as your representatives. We deeply regret that the well-meant attempt to avoid the unnecessary turmoil and expense of a contest in your ward has again been unnecessarily frustrated. As we are personally pledged t,e do all in our power to carry Jut the purp)se of the agreement already referred to, we restpcieullv and confidently appeal to you to support us in this object by recording your vote for Mr. William John Forsberg on Monday next." Mr. Forshaw in his address promises "that if anything can be done to relieve the rates or to make the payment of the c ert of paving the streets more easy for thern " it will have his best attention and most cordial support. Mr. SINGLETON in his address alludes to the intention of the Corporation to errect public abattoirs. He con- tends that it is a question which seriously affects the master butchers, and being an important body of traders they think it only just they should have a representative to look to their interests in this matter. He has had several years' experience in municipal matters, and in this respect claims to have a distinct advantage over his opponents. He contends that under the present system of electing councillora to fill vacancies the who!. of the ratepayers are practically disfranchised. This he considers unjust, and should he be elected he will endeavour to serve the interests of all classes (in- dependent of party er politics),particularly the burgesses of this ward'

The poll opened at eight o'clock in Kendeek-street Infant School. The presiding officers were Messrs Stanley Wilson and F Timperley, and the poll clerks, Messrs H P Brierloy and T El Spinka. Considerable interest was taken in the contest, and at night the vicinity of the palling station presented a busy spectacle. Mr. Forshaw had the assistance of several Liberal workers, including Mr. Clayton, the agent. The butchers on the other band stronely supported their candidate and freely lent him their vehicles.

Result of the Polling. The Maxon wh) is the returning officer of the ward annnuneKl the result from the Town Hall seeps shortly after 830 p.m. The following are the figures : W. J. Forsha,w 11.iiry Singleton 240 Francis Dixon 2O

The counting was conducted in the prPsence of the Mayor (who actod a,s returning officer), Aldermen Sut- ton and Heaton, C3unclllor3 Sinethurat, Burton, Snill- - John Evans, Greening and John Roberts ; Mossro. Forshaw anrt Sinoeton (candidates) ; Mr John Clayton (Liberal ant), Mr. Willi-.in Holbrook (Conservative agent), the Th.cm Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle) and the Deputy T )wn Clerk (Mr. Stanley Wilson) and oth9rs. Prior to the announnment from the Town Hall steps Mayou declared Mr Forshaw to have been duly elected.

Councillor FORSHAW said he should fail in hie duty if he did not propose a vote of thanks to their worthy May4r for the great impartiality and courtesy he had displayei during the election, which had been conducted in a very triendly spirit. (Hear. hear.) Great praise was due to the Town Clerk and to the presiding officers. (Hear, hear.) Mr. SINGLRTON, in secondinz the motion, remarked that lao was v. ry much pleased with the friendly manner in which the election bad beeh fought. Be had been in- terested in several contests of a similar character, but never in one which had been conducted in such a friendly manner. He had not done as well as he had expected, but he and his friends had f,ught a good fight considering the organization against them They had been beaten, but they would certainly come forward on another occasion. (Hear, hear, and laughter). The MAYOR, in reply, said he was glad to find that that spirit of Englianmen which had done so much for them in South Africa during the parr, few months pre- vailed in Warrington. He hoped tha,, Mr. Singleton would not be discouraged by his defeat that day, but that he would come forward again when opportunity offered. He was glad to know that the good fe ?ling which had existed for many years at tla,se elections was continued, preventing the unpleasantness which was sometimes heard of elsewhere. He should like to ack- nowledge the aisle assistance which the Town Clerk and his excellent staff always rendered on these occasions. (Hear, hear.) Speeches at the Conservative Club.
Several speeches were afterwards made at the Con- servative Clun.

Couccillor FORSIZAW, who was warmly cheered, said he desired to th tnk all preseet for the splendid work which had been done that day—work which showed what could be done when the voters put their shoulders to the wheel. He thanked both political parties—Con- servatives and Liberals—who had given him consider- able help, and who bad not returned him by a small majority but by a very substantial one, it was, in fact, a majority that should prevent any other candidate

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
CRICKET

Beautiful weather favoured the match between War- rington and Northern which took place at Arpley on Saturday. The visitors were strongly represented their team including the Rev. J Burrough, who distine.uished himself as a player for Cambridge University. Warring- ton lacked the services of E A Connor.

The Rev J Burrough and W D Lloyd batted first for the visitors the bowlers being Thewlis and G Clarke. With the total at 14 Thewlis accepted an easy return from Lloyd, making way for J W Lashmar. Runs came freely, and Dr. Smith relieved Clarke at 36, but the 50 was soon hnisted after as many minutes play. Both batsmen cont,nued to play with freedom,and J W Bibby took the bill from Dr. Smith a confident appeal made or a breach of rule 24 being answered in the rev, gentle- man's favour. At 84 Clarke again resumed, and in his second over, broke through Lashmar's defence, for a capital 39. Another fine stand was made, wten F G Thompson joined Burrough, and the bowling was fairly collared. W H Podmore was tried with no success, and Burrough completed his 50. At 148 the initial batsms.n was caught at mid-off, bis 71 including one five and eight boundary strokes.

Both G Holt and W K Feraie each bad short innings, but S. E. Job assisted Thompson to take the aggregate to 205, when the closure was applied, Thompson being not out 65 Warrington commenced their innings with B Si!cock and Thewl44 Henson and S E Job sharing the bowling. Runs came steadily from the first, but with the score at 14 a fine bail from the amateur sent back the Warrington professional. J Callon came next, and whereas Silcock exhibited a sound defence, Callon batted with marked freedom. At 43 the RevlJ Burrough was tried at Job's end, and on his second over a fine ball disturbed Callon's off stump. Matters now went badly for the home side, for after Dr. Smith had been sPnt back at 60, three wickets tell at 72, G Clarke after contributing seven, and F C Johnson and J Thompson, without scoring.

Connor did not give much trouble, and the hopes of Warrington saving the match looked forlorn, seeing that there was three-quarters of an hour yet to play, and only two wickets to fall. W. H. Pedsnore joined Si!cock, and whilst the latter exhibited a valuable defence, the last corner played all the bowling with a confidence and freedom which could not hiilp but be admired. Podmnre was particularly revere on Burrough, and a fine stroke to the leg boundary caused the century to ba hoist d. Runs came freely, and Heeson was tried at 113, sending down some tempting balls, which failed to draw the batsmen. F. G. Thompson was tried at 120, whilst a few minutes from seven o'clsck Burrough relieved Hen- son, and succeeded in getting Silcock caught at point. SiWeek has never played a more valuable innings, and there was not a bad stroke during his long stay at the wickets. His defence was exceptionally strong, and to him and Podmore belong the honours. [lampoon whipped in to play out the over, and stumps were drawn with the score at 140 for the loss of nine wickets. Podmore's innings of 43 was indeed a plucky dial:A .7, and coming as it did when matters were going so badly for his side made the contribution all the more valuable.
Death of Mr. H. Gittems.

The death took place on Friday evening of Mr. H. Gittens, of the Battis Hotel, Saukey—treet. The deceased had been ailing some months, and serious complications ensuing a few weeks ago, he took to his bed, and despite all that medical aid could do he passed away at nine o'cleck on Friday night. Mr. Gittens was well-known in the town, and his death will ba regretted by many friends. The funeral, which was largely attended, took place on Tuesday.

SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY.
Services in Parr Hall.

This auspicious event in connection with the above school was celebrated on Sunday And both in point of attendance and in the amount realised was more success- ful than on any previous occasion. The preacher was the Rev. J. Grange Bennett, an evangelist in the Wesleyan denomination, and who is locally connected. For several yea:s now the Sankey Bridges friends have I secured his services and he has always given every satisfaction. The morning service was conducted in the chapel at Sankey Bridges and was well attended. For the afternoon and evening services Parr Hall had been specially engaged and at the evening service this spacious hall was found too small and many were unable to gain admission. The children were arranged on the platform and under the able conductorship of Mr. Walter Brough,the superintendent of the school,they sang very sweetly a number of hymns and choruses. ' Several of tunes had a martial air about them a and the boys distinguished themselves by their vigorous render- ing of the music. Madame Conway who has appeared before the public of Warrington on many occasions sang very acceptably at both the afternoon and evening ser- vices and the audience showed their appreciation by hearty applause. Miss H. Brough gave an excellent interpretation of the song "The King of Love my Shepherd is " and also sang the solo in "I love to sing of Jesus." Mr. T. Brough presided at the organ and Mr. E. Wilkes, A.L.C.M. accompanied on the piano. Miss Morrell very feelingly recited " The last hymn "and a good Effect was pronounced by the organist accompany- ing a portion of the reci:ell.

I The Ceteremerr at the afternoon service was Mr. James Dodds, who delivered a brief addrese. Be said he should like to congratulate the Sankeyßridges Wesleyan friends , upon that magnificent gathering, and upon the efficiency of the choir under the leadership of his good friend Mr. Brough. He felt be must with them "God speed " in the splendid work they were doing at that end of War- rington, and also success not only in their present enter- prise but in their future work. It seemed to him Mr. Brough had the magnetic power of infusing into others that earnestness and sincerity which characterized him- self and whicitwere the bases of all successful work in great causes. He hoped Mr. Brough would live to inspire thousands by his grand example. He (the speaker) knew he had the sympathy of every person in that room and they nould support him. In Sunday schools they should have men who would teach the children the principles which were to make them better citizens and better followers of the Lord and Master—the principles of justice and truth, mercy and peace, which to-day seemed to be in the back ground even among Christian men and Christian ministers. A philosopher said the other day that peace was the dream of the wise, but war was the history of the world. So it was. Yesterday,there was the peace conference at the Hague, to-day that terrible wicked war in South Africa. Let us see to-day that in all these conflicts we had right on our side. H. was speaking the other day to one of their chief Wesleyan ministers—the Rev. Dr. Agar Beet. He said "I am much concerned about this question. I should like to be on the side which. 50 years hence, history will say was the right side. lam not sure that history will say that we were on the right side." Neither was he (the ste-ake.r.) He hoped that in spite of the spirit of militari,m and bastard imperialism which seeme I to be spreading amongst them that they would not forge- that the Master had taught them better things, and they should try and spread peace among nations. Without saying that one side or the other was right, he believed that the war was a great crime against humanity. The total amount realized was £4l 10s, which was in excess of any previous celtections. Annual Tea Meeting.

The annual congregational tea meeting was held in the schoolroom on Monday evening. A good number sat down to a capital tea tun tables being presided over by Mesdames Brough, Blythe, Hardinz,and Misses Coradine Morrell, Boon, Jackson and Highly. After tea an enter- tainment was held, the Rev. C. H. Hocken presiding. The CHAIRMAN in his opening remarks referred to the services held in Parr Hall and said they were a splendid success. That gathering was held so that members of the congregation might show their sympathy with the work that was being carried on in the Sun- day school. He did not think there was any more popular branch of Christian work than that which was done in the Sunday Schools. No anniversaries were signalised by such large gatherings or such large collections. There were more than a million scholars gaining instruction in their Wesleyan Sunday Schools and that was a very striking fact. The rev gentleman proceeded to speak of the responsibilities of teachers and said they should pay particular attention to the spiritual interests of the children. His profound impression was that teachers were not fit for the work unless they were converted to God. The programme was then proceeded with, being taken patt in by Miss H Brough, Miss Alice Morrell, Mr John Thorley and Mr Geldard. Mr E Wilkes accompanied.

div.head: MEN AT HOME. ---- A Word on Their Responsibilities.
div.p: THE MEN AT HOME. ---- A Word on Their Responsibilities.

HEAVY responsibilities, u,ually In the form of wife and children, have alone restrained many men from offering themselves for service in South Africa, and thousands are fuming over the thought that they are not doing their share as Britons. But, by fulfilling their duty at home, these men are acting in the best way possible, though often that in itself becomes no easy matter. One core deserving of sympathy is that of a Leicester man named James Meascm, living at 22, Middle Street. Be is employed as " fettlar " in a Leicester wool factory, and at an age when strong men ar, in their prime—forty years—le gradually fell sick and ailing. " A great weakm S 3 came upon me," be said : " I lost my appetite, I b came so debilitated that I could hardly walk about, and I lost two or three stone in weight. The complaint affected my chest and breath, and I suffered NA ith a severe cough." "I was under one medical man for nine months, but the nature of my illness was never stated on the certi- ficates. Iwa just in that weak and sick state, not able to work or get about ; I was dreadfully worried, for I bad never felt like it before. As time went on I became even worse, nd the outlook was very gloomy for me,for doctors seemed to do me no good. Ido not like to think what would have befallen me had not my mother per- suaded me tp try a box of Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people. She had read of many people cured by these pills, and bought the first lot for me. I commenced to take them, and by the time I had finished the eontents of that box I began to feel stronger and better, and as though a weight had been lifted tom my shoulders. I continued with the pills, taking six leAres altogether. Remember I had been laid up unable to work for nine months, but I went back to work after tak:ng three le3xes of Dr. Williams' pink pills. That was months ago, and I have been gaining my old strength and health ever since. lam as smart as any man at my work, and I can truly say that I feel as right as pessible. I've recommended Dr. Williams' pink pills to mores of people. They have done my wife good as well. For several years she suffered frrquently with severe pains in her head, but the pills have set her up in health."

Mrs. Measom, a lady forty-three years of age, con- firmed the latter eta merit. stating : "We have tried all sorts of medicine, but nothing is like Dr. Williams' pink pills. I had three boxes, and they seemed to put new life into me." Here the interview ended. The enthusiastic remarks of Mr. and Mrs. Wagon aff :rd clear prcof of the beneficial effects of Dr. Wil- liams' pink pil's upon both men and women. The secret of their succe,s lies in the fact that they cure the cause of weakness and disease, not merely acting to relieve the symptoms. In the ea-es cited above Dr. Williams' pink pi le restnred tone:to the nervous system and enriched the exile! b'ed blood. Acting the same way these pills have cured thousands of cases of ar xmia, general weakness, loss of appetite, palpitation, shortness of breath, early decay, all for MP of female weakm ss, hysteria, paralysis, locomotor ataxy, rheumatism, sciatica, scrofula, rickets, chronic erysipelas, consumption of the bowels and lungs. Fhese pills are tonic in action, and are not purgative, but they are genuine only with full name Dr. Will!ams' pink pills for pale people (apvFn words), and are sold by most retai'ers, and Dr. Williahas' Meoicine Company, Holborn 17:adu,:t, London, at two shillings and nine- pence a box, or fix boxes for thirtPen and nine, post free. The New Vicar of Great Sankey. The Rev. J. Roger Jones, who has for eight years officiated as curate of St. Mary's, Great Sankey, has been offered and has accepted the above living, which was renrlt2red vacant by the resignation, through indispaaftiou, of the Rev E. S. Jackson. The patron is Lori !iord. Mr. Jones has held curacies at Farr, Rainford, Widnes, and Forowerth. The living was offered to him in response to a unanim- ous request forwarded to the patron by the parish- ioners. He i 4 a graduate of Trinity College,Dublin. Be took his B.A. degree in 1884 and his M.A. in 1892, and was ordained by the Bishop of Liverpool to ;it. Mary's, Widnes, in 1866. Mr. Jones expresses himself in favour of the appointment of clergymen by the laity, and in the present instance this has practically been_tke case.

div.p: otila•
THE ELA AiN

WITH every succeeding The irthday Queen's year of her gracious reign B. the QUEEN is more en- deared to her people. On this, her eighty-first birthday, she is nearer to us than she was a year 44g0, and many things have happened to make us regard her with more intense affeetion and with a rilere comprehensive patriotism. What a marvel- lous training she has had in public affairs! From the timid young QUEEN, tearfully and prayerfully accepting her high responsibilities, to the mature arkd venerable Lady, deciding on her own initiative to visit Ireland, and to show her high appreciation of the services of her valiant Irish soldiers, what ah enormous span of years, of events, of national arid Imperial development! Always true to the Constitution, as courteous to one set of political advisers as to another, she has lived a Varied, picturesque, and wonderful life. There 18 no Sovereign her senior in Europe, and hence she is revered with more than the customary awe that engirds a Royal Throne. Waves of anti:monarchial feeling have swept oversome other countries, producing convulsions and revolutions. The happy fate of Great Britain has been to see these shocks and to remain calm. A good deal of this serenity is due to the fine personal character 411 d pure domestic life of the QUEEN herself. We banat all cheerfully admit that this is so, and observers on the Continent are perhaps more ready to dwell upon this aspect of the matter than upon %113' other, because of contrasts and experiences to Which we need not more specially refer. The QuEP.3.r, however, has been assisted by wise states- /31°u, and some of them, regarded at the time Waith misgivings by the Constitutional party, have (4ne an immense amount of permanent work 111 avoiding revolution. Popular injustice and im- -I"orishrnent will breed evils out of which only the lit 43' of violence is discerned. It has not been so in IS country. Our tumults have been against 14411.°W-minded politics, and not against the Mon- witellY. It has never been possible to confound the 4:llarch with the Ministry, and on the only asieu when the Monarch hesitated, the states- of 410 time saved the sit,uation. The QUEEN erSelf ooking back with quiet dignity over the 14arvell0119 records of her long life, cannot see „ uch, if anything, in her public life to regret. As YErEuN, mother, and widow she has exhibited solid and endearing virtues. Troubles have come, but they have left her personally unscathed. She has borne herself bravely under all the personal and national trials which have occurred in a reign of ever sixty years. To-day finds her of a ripe age and Wisdom, full of generous feelings, living close to the nation's heart, and bearing up bravely under the burden of physical infirmities and the weight of Empire. Her vitality has been extraordinary, and we cannot help marvelling at it. Birth counts something, but intellectual activity, careful tiving, variety of life, interest in what is going on, " it political, literary, artistic, or social, have *Misted to endow her with powers beyond the "linary. We acknowledge the bright force of her z"alnPle. Science and sanitation are guarantee- to ordinary Englishmen a longer average life. 4.14 QUEEN, in her own person, is an exemplar of the advance we are making. She has entered upon another decade as fresh as she was several years 1140; and the coming century will, we hope, find Or QUEEN of Englmid,and better loved than ever. A life so wonderful and bright is rare, and we shall all heartily and unreservedly join in the good old Wish, that she may have Many Happy Returns % The Day!

IMPERIAL enthusiasm flthusiasm and its never gauged higher than Dangers. it does at the present blcunent. The war is entering upon its final 111148 es, and the long-pent-up emotions of the iben, Pie are finding natural and exuberant expres- 'cln• There is something delightful in the depth, Unanimity, and sincerity of this enthusiasm. We :°llld not do anything to check it. It is good- °Mß:lured, there is little that is vindictive in it, 411c1 it is quite consistent with a merciful ending 1:11! a great struggle. Convinced that the war cln 'a'Ve but one ending, ready to do justice to every 4., et of British and Colonial heroism, and recognis- N that the Boers have displayed bravery and 40dihood, it may bo questioned whether there are 4113? dangers in such national, spontaneous, and illevated enthusiasm. Our foreign friends and foes 41.43 ready to admit that there is nothing extra- and morbid in the joy which has been "trobbing all over the Empire. It makes us :Ile in aim and feeling, in appreciation of valour 4U. endurance, in admiration of resourcefulness, ,LBciPline, and success. The cold nature of the t'Ple has been melted under the warmth of ecess, and amidst all these exhilarating mani- -4:statioes there is nothing of vohemence, or rage 07d revenge. Probably this is the greatest feature th the whole demonstration. Everybody is satisfied at We shall win, and that right speedily, and iatii°erYbody hopes that the beaten foe will realise at, great as have been his sacrifices in men and 14(4163', the British and the Colonial victors have vll4 sacrifices as great, and will win from history ;verdict of a just and generous appreciation. th...,t We might have feared was a vainglorious t of militarism, a feeling that we had become toxiineinie, and that the glory of war was too in- n etos 'ating to be resisted. Happily, no trace oti'd yet be found of these morbid emotions to tendencies. We hope they may continue be be conspicuous by their absence. It would hitea Pity if the pure joy of gratitude for a deliverance from peril and suffering should

degenerate into a craving for a life full of the like excitements, and for more adventures, in order that critics should be silenced, the unfriendly punished, and the world made to feel the might of the British Empire. We do not want any sigh- ing for more enemies to conquer, or for more ex- tended adventures in the field of war. We are an industrial people, not versed in the scientific arts of war, and mainly acting on the defensive in the little wars we are so often called upon to wage in various parts of our Empire. It is for the sake of the Empire, and not for the sake of :the mere lust of con- quest, the tiger-thirst for slaughter, that we have engaged in the great struggle now happily drawing to a cicse. It would be a sad thing to see our enthusiasm turned to improper uses, and made to do the dirty work of some of the Con- tinental Powers, who would gladly see us embroiled with some of our neighbours. The busi- ness of true patriots just now is te keep enthusiasm in the right channels, to preserve it from the direc- tionlof greedy capitalists, and the inspiration of the military mischief-makers. When the war is over we shall want to attend to the pacific re argan- isation of the army, in the interests of defence, and to settle down with our colonies in the new spirit of family affection and devotion which the war has developed. We shall have some big bills to meet, some grave problems to settle, and some need for all the calmness and sound judgment which are endangered by great excitement and railitary fervour. We have shown that our hearts are right. Let our manhood now have free and wise play.

The statue of Mr. Gladstone, unveiled in the Central Hall of the House of Commons, is acknow- ledged by the Parliamentarians to be in every way worthy of the great subject. In that respect it differs from the representation of Mr. John Bright which, figuring the Tribune in his old age, failed to give that impression of vigour and oratorical power which always characterised him when ad- dressing the Chamber. Sculptors suffer from a disadvantage as compared with painters, because they cannot take artistic liberties, and they can obtain no assistance by a choice of back-ground. In the portrait the distribution of the light may make or mar draughtsmanship. In sculpture the artist receives no such assistance. The great becret of Professor Herkomer's success is in the skill with which he focuses attention on the face and, makes the likeness a speaking one. He has done that with a plain type in the New Gallery this year, and it is wonderful. In the cold marble, of course, much may be achieved by pose, and Mr. Pomeroy has been very fortunate in striking upon a familiar, and, at the same time, effective attitude of the ex-Premier; but, of course, the flush of the cheeks and the glance of the eye which marked the old man eloquent were beyond him. A canvas by Watts, done in his broad strong method of a de- cade or so ago, would have been far more appeal- ing to the public. Who can forget his portrait of Carlyle which adorns the National Gallery, with its thick impasto and its strength of judgment as to the characteristics of the sage of Chelsea ? Still, for those who knew him well the carving of the ex-Premier will be an arresting piece of work ;and for others who compare the expression of pictures with the verisimilitude of figure, it will complete the conception.

The people of this part of the country generally, and Manchester and Liverpool in particular are somewhat disappointed in their hopes of rapid communication by the rejection of the measure before Parliament, but have at least one source of satisfaction. The committee have reported in favour of the principle of their novel scheme. This is for a mono-line; the power to be supplied by electricity, the rate of speed to be ninety miles an hour. The critics who cast doubt on the practica- bility of the proposal should remember that the two cities have from the early days of railway history been distinguished for their enterrrise in engineering feats, and that these schemes have always been scoffed at in the first in- stance. Aged residents can tell of the ridicule with which the railway competition of 1829 was received. The course was the same as is now contemplated for the single line, or, at least, the termini were the same. A prize of £5OO was offered. Five locomotives entered for the stakes, and the Rocket, built by the Brothers Stephenson. carried off the prize. It accomplished the distance at the then incredulously quick average rate of thirteen miles and forty-two yards per hour. It was thought to be dangerous, but it was done. In that charming book, "The History of our Civilisa- tion," only five years ago Mr. Salnuelson,the editor pointed with pride and satisfaction to the triumphs of engineering science. To-day, he said, an average speed of forty-seven miles and thirty yards is attained. Now, short as is the interval of time that has passed, we appear to be On the point of doubling that record. Sir John Kennaway was the chairman of the committee which looked into the project submitted. and, himself a railway direc- tor of experience, had no doubt that the idea would became feasible in the near future. Such a scheme, of course, if it were generally adaptable would largely decrease the cost of road-makiwz, and its value commercially would be enormous. But the first journeys would again alarm the timid.

Mr. Jenner Fast had very little of moment to suggest to the members of the Warrington Beard of Guardians at their last meeting in the way of improvement. With the opening of the new in- firmary it is to be hoped that we have for ever left behind us the long-standing complaint of over- crowding. The probability seems to be that the Guardians will have laid themselves open to the charge of having too much "roominess," for it is very questionable if there will ever be sufficient patients to fill the capacious infirmary just nearing 1 completion. However the fault is in the right direction. Mr. Fast poked a little fan at the fire escapes in use at the Workhouse. The fire escape from the upper storeys appears to be a shut() to be thrown out of the window, through which the inmates are expected to slide to the ground below. The feasibility of this means of escape has not been thoroughly tes- ted at the Workhouse, and Mr. Fast is kind enough to inform us that there is a great objec- tion to test its qualities. We can readily appreeiate the diffidence shown, especially by the female inmates, -to be dropped head foremost or even fot foremost down a tube forty or fifty feet long. Even Workhouse inmates have feelings and dacliee to be passed through a baker's shute like a pack of flour. We are afraid that in case of fire, the means of escape provided by the Guardians would be found useless in the case of many of the in- mates and Mr. Fast is entitled to direct the attention of the Guardians to the need of a better and let us hope, a more humane means of escape.

The newspaper press in Warrington has had a I chequered career since the Brothers Eyres first I undertook to provide Warrington with a weekly newspaper in March, 1756. "Eyres Weekly Journal or Warrington Advertiser" was one of the earliest newspapers in the provinces and we believe there was only one other newspaper in Lan- cashire at that time. But the enterprise of the Brothers Eyres was ill requited for the paper only lived a few months. The sad experience of these first caterers of news for the Warrington public has been the experience of many another newspaper proprietor in this town since those early days, and we are reminded of this by the death which we record this week of Mr. George Powlson, who was editor and proprietor of the now defunct "Warrington Advertiser." It is about ten years since Mr. Powlson took farewell of the Warri ng,t )n public and brought the career of the " Warrington Advertiser" to a close. His newspaper was never what may be termed a financial success, hut des- pite all the difficulties which beset hiea Mr. Powl- son won the admiration of many Warriuo,ton friends by the independent line he took on public, and more particularly local questions.

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY, MAY 25, 1900.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, MAY 25, 1900.
RUNCORN NOTES.

[BY A CORRESPONDENT]. The report of the Runcorn Rural District Council meeting provides us with a view of the rivers pollution question, as affecting the Manchester Ship Canal. Writing some months age I stated it would be interesting to know whether the Manchester Ship Canal is a stream within the meaning of the Act. Some people contend it is a river pure and simple; others it is a canal in its upper reaches, and a river from Latchford to Eastham for the reason
that it is tidal (more or less) for that distance. The point, however, will have to be decided by a law COWL.

There is ens thing pretty clear,however, and that is as to the extent the canal has been used as a sewage outlet. Indeed it is notorious that the effluvia that assails one in its upper reaches has for some time been most objectionable,and in the inter- ests of the public health something will have to be done. That the Rivers Pollution Act will bring it about is also pretty clear, for whatever the canal may prove to be, the streams emptying into it will be regulated by the Act, and the cleansing of those will go a long way to purify the canal. The developments of the question will be watched with keen interest.

I learn, on good authority, that the County Coun- cil are willing to put things in ship-shape order so far as the Astmoor Bridge is concerned, provided, of course, the landlord will part with the necessary site for the naw bridge. They don't mean that the landlord should give it them either, and are willing to pay a fair price, but anyone can see that to ask £1,500 for the requisite terra firma is putting it on very heavy. It is to be hoped for the public good some satisfactory figure can be arrived at, and that too whilst the County Council are of the opinion and policy they now express regarding it.

The re:joicings in and around Runcorn are for a time over, but will no doubt be re- newed on the slightest occasion. A characteris- tic of the last lot was the lack of organisation. After the invitation of the Chairman of the Urban District Council to " come and rejoice" was issued it appears that nothing further was done. Every- one " sat tight," as it were. waiting for his neigh- bour to start, or wondering what was to appear next. The formation of a provisional committee, and a little organisation would have considerably enhanced all the pleasure and would have done away with the feelings of dissatisfaction which were felt by many.

Our little town is being gradually improved in the matter of streets and sanitation ; yet there still remains a great deal to be accomplished. Indeed the room for improvement is so great that it must be years before Runcorn will reach even a low standard of efficiency in these matters. It is very gratifying, therefore, to note, with regard t 3 public health, Runcorn and district can take a very high place and can boast a mortality and a very low average indeed.

div.head: RUNCORN PRINTING WORKS AND
div.p: A RUNCORN PRINTING WORKS AND
THE FACTORY ACTS.

At Runcorn Petty Sessioas on Monday, before Messrs F. J. Norman and W. Handley, Richard Moore and Company, printers, Ilieh-street, were sumenened for committing a breach of the Factory Acts of 1873 and 1893 by neglecting to securely fence certain dangerous parts of the machinere, wnereby Eleanor Ellison suffered bodily injuey. Mr R. E. Graves, chief inspector of factories, Liverpool, prosecuted.—Sydney Erawt, an in- spector. deposed that he visited the defendants' factory on the 29th March in consequence!) of an accident there on the 9:h of that month. Mr. Moore was not presnr, and he (witness) was shown round the factory by some- one r.presenting him. He saw the girl Ellison who told him she bad her fingers trapped in the cog wheels of a printing and cutting machine. He examined the an .chiiie and in his opinion the cog wheels were dangerous and ought to have been protected. The wheels were ex- p,ised very much. The girl Ellison had not been passed by the doctor.—Eleanor Ellison deposed that she was 13 years of age. On the 9th Marsh she was straightenieg wrappers near to this machine. When the girl in charge of the machine was taking the wrappers off the machine she (witness) had to put her foot on the treadle of the machine. She did not know how she get her finger in the wheels, but she felt the end jerked off and then she fainted. She had te do what Sarah Basnott, who was in charge of the machine, told her. Se had not been examined by Dr. McDougall, the e.rified surgeon. She had worked for 11:33SrA. Hoare since the 4th De member last.—Cress-examined by Mr. Moore, she denied thac she had been warned about these wheels.—Mr. Moore, sworn, said he obtained the machine a little over 18 months ago. RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL

The usual fortnightly mee:lng of this Council was held at the Workhouse, Dutton, on Tuesday. There were present :—Mr Joseph Koowles (chairman), Admiral Jones-Parry, Messrs J Stokes, S Woodward, T Wright, J Mclntyre, P Gleave, T Lewis, W Fletcher, J Spruce, E Clarke, W Bradford, W Turner,T Darlington, J Moseley- Williams, with Mr George F Ashton (clerk), Mr W E Hough (assistant clerk), Messrs W Dig,gle and J Swinton (surveyors), Mr James Farrington (inspector), and Dr J Adams (medical officer).

THE THELWALL BROOX .-A SERIOUS COMPLAINT. Mr R A Naylor, Cuerden Hall, thelwall, Warrington, mocks. date May 11th, wrote as follows to Mr. Jame.' Farringtoa (the council's inspector):—"Dear Sir.—l would be glad it you could make an appointment to see me here, respecting the nuisance arising from the tanyard. I am advised the wisest course would be for me to bring down some Government experts. I have now ascer- tained the cause ot the nuisance which has existed for some years, but which is now increasing in intensity. It appears this is due to the increased use of chemicals some of which appear to be of a highly poisonous character. Perhaps you will make an early appoint- ment."
Mr. Farrington had forwarded the above to the Clerk

(NIL George F Ashton) to which he had replied. Mr. Naylor had replied to Mr. Ashton as follows : " Dear Sir :—I am glad to hear from you that your Council will have the matter brought bafere them at their next meeting. Would you like my coachman, who appears to have been the greatest sufferer to explain his case in person. Some three years ago he and his wife almost lost their lives through this nuisance. It has now been going on sAne four years and although it is not continuous still it is very bad when the poisonous refuse is allowed to flow down the brook."
The Clerk stated that he had replied to Mr. Naylor that the council would not require anyone to attend before them until they requested it. In further reply to which Mr. R. A. _ Naylor. wrote

(19th May) "Hoping the Council would have the Brook cleaned quickly. Even the roadntan had to leave his work alongside it ; the smell being so offensive. The liquid sent down it must be of a very poisonous charac- ter."
The Clerk: Tire brook is the one that the Highway sab4comraittee saw when going their rounds. Mr. Woodward : I propose that those letters be re-
ferrsd to the enadical officer of health. Mr. E. Clarke seconded and the proposition was unani- mously carried.

"NAME YOUR own houses !" The following letter was read by the Clerk : Latchford, Warringt-m, May 12, 1900. Gentimam— Of late the residences in your rural districts have materially increased, and as great inconvenience is ex- perienced as to the names of our roads and streets and I lanes I bPg respectfully to invite your attention to the difficulty of having no known addresses, Amongst several I woald name the Chester-road, which used to bo callrd the" Chester-road," but is now transferred into " Grappenhali-rnai." This is the road from the Dog and Dart to the Mullvrry Tree and indeed on to Walton. The road in which I live was always called the Grappelli- hall-road and ran from Mr. Milling's cornerdown to near the Cheshire Cheese. I have now lived sixteen years in my present house but have not been able to give any distinctive address to those at a distance with whom I I may have communications. Could you not have some few good cast iron posts put up and give a general baptism to cur benighted locality at least.—l am, gentle- , risen, yours obediontly, S. CMANDLEY. Mr '3 Woodward : I should advise that gentleman to baptise his own house. That's his remedy. (Laughter.) The next business was proceeded with. Rix ERi POLLUTION.—" IS THEE SKIP CANAL A RIVER ?

Mr Reginald Potts, clerk of the Counts, Council, wrote under date 19 May,l9oo,as follows :—"Dear Sir,—Rivers Podution,—Referring to your letter of the 12th Jemmy last and the cony report of your Rivers Pollution Com- mittee transmitted therewith, I am instructed by the Rivers Pollution Committee of this Council to transmit to you a copy of a report raade to them by the County Mecitcel Officer of Health, and which I do herewith, and to request that your District Council will intimate to M 9 ler the information of my Committee what steps they purpose taking to etop the pollution mentioned by the County Medical Officer of Health." l'he Clerk said that Dr. Vacher, the County Medical Officer, in his report stated .—" The County Medical Officer of Health is of opinion that the Runcorn Rural Di-triet Medical Officer of Health is doing his best to stop the pellotion of rivers and streams in his district, but that as a large proportion of these brosks are practi- cally sewers discharging into the Manchester Ship Canal (e.g., Walton Brook, Helton Brook, Woods Row Brook, &c), unless it he deeided that the Manchester Ship Canal is a stream within the meaning of the Rivers Pollu- tion Act, 1876, action taken for the cleansing of the said brooks may not be successful. The two most marked instances of pollution noted by the District Medical Officer of Health are those from Messrs. Ockleston's and Mr. Reynolds's tanneries. If such bad effioents as these cannot be kept out of the Manchester Sop Canal at Run- corn, it will be difficult to prevent ordinary sewage from entering the Canal in the Runeorn District. How- ever, the County medical officer thinks it should be pointed out to the District Medical Officer that to some extent the results he obtained are misleading. In some instances a sample of a brook was taken for analysis, and on this being certified "a first class effhent," it seems to have been inferred that nothing was wrong. For example, between Sutton and Higher Whitley, are 20 houses drained by a common sewer to a ditch which discharges into Norcot Brook and the same brook is also pollu col by receiving the drainage of 12 other houses ; a sample of the buck is analysed and reported " a first class effl ant," and this seems to have been regarded as evidence that there was ne pollution which should be stopped. If, instead of sampling the brook, the owners of the 20 houses and the 12 houses had been required to effectue'ly treat their sewage, the cleansing of tile broe!: might have been accomplished. To give one more oxample, in the parish of Kingsley (having at last census 245 Mouses) nearly half the houses are sewered directly or indirectly into Kingsley brook, instead of getting those house-drains cut off from the brook, and the sewage treated at sewage disposal works. A sample of the brook is analysed and pronounced "A first class effluent," which appears to have satisfied the local authorities." The matter was ref ,rred to the River's Pollution Com- mittee.

In answer to a request for a concise definition of his policy upon (1) The Punishment Clause ; (2) Tho B 1 (..;tc Grar, Foes System ; and (3) Tenura of Pffic af Fllernentary School Teachars. Sir J. T. Brunner, Bart., M.P., favours us with the follow- ing .
9, Ennismore-gArdens, S.-W., May 19 h, 1900. To the Editor of the " Examiner."

Dear !;ir,—My time is so much occupied that I can answer your queries only in cult fashion. 1. I are of opinion that it is the clear and obvious 'hey of every high ',minded teacher to sub- mit to and even to welcome the sli4ht restriction on their piwer invr)lved in the necessity of making a record of even- ca.e ot corporal punishment.

2. The Mock Gr-intis a wholesome relief from a system which, whiht it has done good work is now out of date, but I utterly disapprove of the lowering of the total grant to the best schools. 3. What I have said of the high-minded teacher in relation to the power of inflicting corporal punish • men*, applies viti even greater strength to the public-spiriteO Achool manager with regard to his power to dismiss a teacher. The argument I have said is stronger in the case of the manager than in that of the teacher, and that for the reason that the teacher ig the servant of the public, by whom he is paid, and not the servant of the manoger. Arbitrary power 151 good for none of us, neither for those who wield it, nor for those who are subject to it.---Yours faithfully,
JOHN T. BRUNNER.

div.head: QUEEN'S BIRTHDAY.
div.p: THE QUEEN'S BIRTHDAY.

Runcorn and Widees and the whole neighbouring dis- tricts, gave Thursday last to the Queen in the true liberal sense. A aeneral holiday was proclaimed, and indulged in to the fullest by all and ever;one. Both towns were deoorated from end to end. Flags and bunting and jollification were tha orders for the day,and from early morning troops of youngsters paraded the streets with the inevitatele " rin Pot Bands " and Kruger effigies. The national colours and standards appeared everywhere and tradesmen vied with each other in decorating their several business premises. Portraits of Her Mejesty and Lord Roberts we:e also com- mon and appeared prominently in all the embeliehments as well as red,white and blue,aed the whole air was pervaded witt a loyal patriotic spirit. Au enterprieing shoemaker had displayed beneath his sign-board "Bravo Victoria, 81 not out, may uhe make the century," and everyone that passed echoed the sentiment. There were processions in both towns and at night Widnes presented a brilliant appearance, and its streets were enlivened with a cycle procession of quite gigantic proportions. Considering the whole lacked somewhat in organisation, all was very good. The Volunteer and other bands were also in considerable evidence and rendered considerable service in enlivening the proceedings. In short the celebration of her Majesty's 814 t birth'ay was obsPrved with a zest and zeal unparalleled in the hirory of either town, a stencil- lion of things brought about, no doubt, be the recent successes of the British Arms in South Atria?, added to the love and veneration in which Her Majesty is every- where held.

EARLESTOWN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.

The 158th quarterly meeting of this Society was held in the Lo-opera ire Hall, Earlestown, on Mon- day evening. Mr. D. Forester presided, and there was a fair attendance of members. The minutes a the last quarterly meeting were read and condrmedi • and the report and balance, which was as foam; was adopted. The cash receipts were shown no £9.538 6s 81, being an increase over last quarter se £619 14s 8d and compared with the correspond nig period last year, an increase of £1,124 94 91i. rho net profits realised are £1,469 193 01 which were dig posed of as follows; to pay a dividend of 3s in tko .£ to merals-rs, which would Absorb £1,441 84 6, and the balance, .£l9 lOs 61d to contingent fund. During the quarter 52 new members had been admitted, and 26 had withdrawn, leaving 1,552 on the register, 1,150 of whom had brought in checks. Messrs, E. Jones and T Swift were re-elected on the Committee of Management. The Committee asked for, and obtained, authority to louse from Lord Newton a plot of land off Cross-lane for the erection of stabling, cart shed, &c. The usual grant in aid of the employees annual trip was sanctioned. A. donation of £2 2s was made to the Old Age Pension League, and a grant of £5 was made towards the Indian Famine fund. A member introduced question affecting the check system, suggesting the reversion to the paper checks which some years ago were in operation, but which were not found to be of workable advantage, After some discussion a motion that no alteration be affected, was carried. unanimously. This was all the business. WARGRAVB CHURCH, EARLNSTOWN.

• The annual speAal services in aid of the War- grave and Vulcan Day Schools were held in the above church, on Sunday. At the morning service the preacher was the Rev Canon •Willink, M.A., vicar of St. Helen', who said that his intention was to preach upon the education question, but in view of the general rejoicing in connection with the re- lief of Mateking, he would direct his remarks upon levsons to be derived from the defence of that place. His discour4e was very interesting and was thoroughly enjoyed by those present. The anthem rendered by the choir was "0 Worship the King.' In the evening the pulpit was occupied by the Rev F A Screston, 8.A., vicar of Christ Church, Latch- ford, whose sermon was of a most instructive and argumentative character. The evening anthem was " Praise the Lord, 0 Jerusalem," and at each ser- vice special hymns were sung by the scholars, the National Anthem being sung at the close of each service. In the afternoon an organ recital and musical kervice was given by Mr E Leyland, or- ganist, and the choir. A good programme was sah- mitted, vocal items being given by Miss R Urea Miss Molyneux, Miss Corlett, Mr S Henderson,and ,Mr 3 Molyneux. The collections amounted to a little over £23.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
SAD DOMESTIC FATALITY AT ST. HELENS.

'Mrs. Margaret Fitznatrick, aged seventy-one, died under very painful circumstanees on Monday night. Deceased wee the wife of Robert Fitzpatrick, a retired worka foreman, whose eldest son is confined to bed. Burbling from an internal complaint. On Sunday the patient was brought thwnptairs.and his bed put into the parlour. On Monday it was decided to change the posi- tion of the bed, and to enable this to be done several large pieces of furniture had to be moved. While Mrs. Fttipa,trick's sons and daughters were doing this, a piece of board near a step leading from one kitchen to the other was moved, and she tripped and fell, striking her throat against a chair. BPt tea and daughter attended her, and about four o'clock she went to Dr. Twyford,who gave her instruotions what to do. She returned home, and at half past six Dr. Turnbull was called, and found her in so serious a condition that Dr. Reid was brought to perform an operation. Chloroform was administered preparatory to the operation being performed, but in a few minutes the patient collapsed and died.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES

SHOCKING NEGLECT OF CHILDREN.—PAINFErL CASE. At the Warrington Police Jour:, on Ft iday, before the Mayor and other magistrates, Joseph Towers and Martha Ellen Towers, 17, Ernest-street, were summened for neg- lecting their children, Alice, William, and Amy, in .1 manner likely to cause them unnecessary suffering and irjury to health on April 27th.—Mr Browne prosecuted on behalf of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children. and said that the male defendant was a shoe maker. He had a son who earned 85 per week, and he allowed his wife something like 15t to 18, per week altogether. Mrs Towers was the stepmother of the child Alice, who was in a terrible state. She wore only a frock and two pieces of und rclothine which were filthy dirty and alive with vermin. Her body was one mass of vermin bites and lice were crawl- ing all over her. The back of her head was one mass of sores which were discharging ;natter. The hair was matted and alive with lice, her boots were worn down and altogether she was terribly neglected. The reason why the prosecution had taken place was because the married sister of the girl who lived in Cartwright-stret t had had to look after the children until she was tired. She was determined not to de it any longer and so the Inspector was called in and he called in Dr. Bowden. Another child William aged two and a half years was free from vermin, but the body was dirty and bitten with vermin The left eye was badly inflamed and closed up through want of attention. The child was slightly rickety through want of food. The child Amy was fairly well clothed and in a fairly clean condition. The stench up- stairs was enough to knock anyone down. Evidence was then called —E ten Hannan, Cartright street. the dauehter of Towers said she had had to look after the children. She had had one of them for 18 months now. Her father was quite capable of looking after them. Witness proceeded t o describe the horrible condition of the child Alice.— Lizzie Towers, a daughter of defendant said she NM the child Abce about two months ago and the was then in a dirty ,state.—Inspector Hackett described the state of the children. He dded tt at he went upstairs. The front room was filthy dirty. Mere were two iron bedsteads, etraw mattresses and a flock bed but there was no covering. The b ack room coatained iron bedsteads with a pair of mattresses on. Lice were crawling all over the mattresses. The following day he saw tne mate defendant who said he was sorry for what had oceurred. —Dr Bowden spoke to examining the children.—The male defendant said he did not think the children were in such a bad condition as had been described.—The female defendant said she thought it was a "made up thing." She OW not drink.—The Chairman said the Bench were disposed to give defendants another chance. It was as much for old acquaintance sake as for anything else. The case was a most painful one as he (the chairman) had known Towers so long. The family was a most respectable one and there was no excuse for defendants behaving as they had done. As regarded the wife she said she did not drink. Be was surprised that a sober, able bodied woman should allow the children to get in that state, They would adj men the case for four weeks to give them a chance and if there was not a substantial improvement at the end of that time they should send both the defendants to gaol.
A WARRINGTON TIIIEF AT ST. HELENS.

_ At St. Helens Police Court on Monday, before the Mayor (Councillor Beecham), Alderman J. C. G mble, and Mr. G. W. Rawlins, Rob-rt Hohnes,of Warrington, was charged with stealing 503 in silver,and an overcoat, value 103 from the dwelling-house, 9, Langtree-street, the property of Henry Williams, a coal d-aler —Chief Constable Wood said that on webruary 12 Mr. Williams met the prisoner in Higher Parr-street.and agreed to rake him to help him in the coal business. He was to give him 3s 6d, and to let him live in his (Williams's) house. On the morning of ths 14th, when Williams got up he mis;ed the 503 from his trousers pockets, and also the overcoat from a table, end it was evident that Holmes had gone from his own bedroom into Williams's room and taken the trousers off the bed. On looking about he found the prisoner had left the house. Williams gave information to the police, but Holmes was only arrested by the Warrington pollee on Sunlay, and handed over to Detective Holding, who charged him with the theft. The prisoner admitted stealing 14s in silver and the overcsat: Evidence was given by Williamsand Holding. The bench committed Holmes, who is well connected in Warrington, to prisoner for a month's hard labour.

Her father had given her instructions not to serve the defendant's brother on account of his filthy !ant/nave. On the Saturday night in question complainant served the defendant with a glass of beer. Sir,—l am directed by the LT:cel Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 20th ult., relative to the propo,ed determination of the Rev. J. J. VOLUNTEER INTELLIGENCE. The Annual Encampment.

The battalion orders for the Ist Volunteer Battalion, P.W.V, South Lancashire Regiment contain the follow- ing notifications :—The Battalion will attend brigade camp this year at Conway from 2nd June to the 17th June. An advance party of two sergeants and 15 rank and file are required for the purpose of pitching camp, Names to be given to the Sergeant Major as soon as possible. Only those members who can arrange to remain if necessary, after the breaking up of the Camp will be selected " Marchiag Order for the undermentioned details will be as follows Pioneers : Full marching order the same as the remain- der of the Battalion but without rifles. Band and Buglers : Great coats rolled and strapped to back of waistbelt. Water bottles, haversacks a, d side arms to be carried, but no rifles. Cyclist Section : Drill orders with slung rifles, water bottles and haversacks. Ambu- lance Section : Full marching order the same as remain- der of Battalion, with slung rifles. Transporc Section : Those proceeding with the vehicles will pack their valise equipment and arms in them. Those proceeding with the Battalion will be in full march- ing order the same as the remainder of the Battalion. The advanced party of the Battalion, consisting of Quarter Master Sergeant J Wilcocks, Annourer Sergeant G Davies Sergeant W Wnitfield and 15 rar k and file will parade on Wednesday the 30 h inst at the Drill Hall, Warrington, at 8-30 a.m. under the command of 2nd Lieutenant CL Williamson and Quarter Master A F G Potter and pro- ceed to Conway for duty by the 9.5 a.rn. train. All spare kit tunics, etc., taken to camp this year will be carried in kit bags whicn have been provided for each man and which will henceforth be eonsidored as part of his equipment for which he will be liable to make good any loss or damage except by fair wear. Hit bags should be packed and left at the Drill Hall on Friday night the let June ready for removal. The field kit will be carried in the valise as usual. Nothing but kit bags will be allowed to convey spare kits in to camp. rho Battalion (Church of England party) will parade for Divine Ser- vice .at 9.15 a.m., on the 27th inst., dress dri I order (kersey frocks) with side arms and helmets. Dress for officers review order."

The superintendent (Mr. Samuel Albinsou) gave the connec- tive readings.

div.head: Gospel Hall.
div.p: Gospel Hall.

On Sunday the service was conducted by Mr. Joseph Whitehouse W1:1080 remarks were based on the words of the Propbet Jeremiah 12-5 " How wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan," illustrating the sul2ject by the story of the Israelites, passing over Jordan from the wilder ness into Canaan (see. John 34). Charles Wesley and many others speak of Jordan as death. The ordinary cases and troubles o 1 life often weary and upset us and v. ben unforseen adversity comes in the shve of sickness Ices of employment, lass of money and other causes, we are in a state of despair and so the Prophet asks, " If these things so trouble us, how shall we be in the lwellings of Jordan, wh.'n death takes hold of us? To meet troubles and death in our own strength is an utter failure, but to the Christian; Jordan 'will only be an ' entrance into Heaven.

div.head: Late Rev. James Warnock. Memorial Service.
div.p: The Late Rev. James Warnock. Memorial Service.

A memorial service for the late Rev J Warnock, MA. B D , was held in the S. John's Presbyterian Church, of which the deceated gentleman had been the pastor for 24 years. There was a good congregation. The pulpit which on Sunday evening was draped in black was occupied by the Rev J H Scott, of Ancoats, Manchester (clerk to the Presbytery), who took for his text " Every man in his own order." He remarked that he had been entrusted by the Presbytery to come to that church and speek to them in connection with the passing away of their brother presbyter—the Rev J Warnock. It seemed to be an impertinence to speak to them about one they knew more about than he did, hut they often met in the prosecution of their church work. He supposed that he was right in saying that if there was one thing notice- able about their late pastor it was his selitaairn ss. Ile meant to say that if he was anything more than another, it was that he was a student. To accumulate a vast amount of knowledge he devoted hims-lf with great ardour as a youth in his university and theological course. As a result of this he had earced for himself reputet ion and honour. What he be- gan at college he carried on all through his life. Ho was first a student, second a student, and last a student. It was a revelatien to go into his library and Eel the charact o. of his books. There was one thing that sugges- ted itself to him. To a large extent a great deal of that knowledge was buried in himself. He did not know to what extent he used his pen, or what benefit; his congre- gation hsd had ; some of them might know. He was not prepared to say what he knew, became very few of them could gauge that. He knew that he preachee in such a manner that the youngest of his congregation believed that he was a man worth listening to. He was careful what he preached. They would all agree with him that if there was one thing that distinguished him it was his conscientiousness. Conspicuous again was bis Ezeath Tres of disposition. So quiet seas his dispositian that ha did not press his suggestions as he mieht have done. He gave them to his congregation whether they adopted them or not. Sometimes be did not speak long enough perhaps. It would not do if the world was com- pesed solely of such men. It did not matter what a man's learning was, there were certain things after all which made a man valuable to others, which crinstitu ted a sense of loss when he was removed from them.— The deceased's favourite hymns—" 0 God, our help in ages past "and " Brief life is here our portion "—were sung, and at the close of the service Mr. F. Jonas played the Dead March in " Saul" on the organ. The service was a most impressive one throughout.
Reference by the Rev. J. F. Matthews.

Preaching in the Baptist Chapel, Latchford, on Sunday morning, tha Pastor, the Rev. J. F. Matthews said : Before proceeding to the subject of this morning's ear- min I desire to pay my simple but affectionate tribute to the memory of one of the saintliest men I have ever known. I have not yet beeu in this town tbree years, but very early in my Warrington experience I learnt to admire with deep reverence the lofty character of our deceased friend, and to hold in the highest regard his great intellectual endowments. Few men had a more tender heart, or a more sympathetic spirit. None in this district excelled him in learning. His knowledge was most extensive and most minute. He was familiar with the great masters of our Puritan literature, and knew also the best modern English and foreign works in the sphere of Biblical Criticism. An able scholar, a keen logician, .he possessed a strong critical bent blended with a judgment at once dispassionate and mature. His sense of humour was strong, as is usual in men of his nationality. Be could enjoy a good story and tell one too. To a natural modesty he added the grace of tru. humility: Pie was deficient in the gifts and grace of oratory ; yet the substance of his sermons was ever thoughtful and weighty. They were written in the style of an easy and practised writer. Severely calm as a preacher, without an atom of enthusiasm, there was be- hind all he said the calm sincerity of real conviction. His character was marked by a rare beauty and courtesy. He al waye left on me the impression that he was a man who knew God intimately and delighted to converse with Him. Finally, he was a true example of the devout student, the careful critical scholar and the cultured Christian gentleman. He will be missed by his church, and not lees by the band of Free Church ministers, of whom he was a highly venerated member. I have been honoured by knowing him, and • shall ever prize his memory among the few measures I pesse3s.

div.head: Mill Brow Sunday School, Runcorn.
div.p: Mill Brow Sunday School, Runcorn.
Anniversary Services at Halton-road Chapel.

Last Sunday the anniversary ger vices in connection with the Mill Brow Sunday Schools w(re held at Balton- road Wesleyan Chapel, Runcorn, and were attended by targe concri,gations. The preacher was the Rev. J. Hanby Bradford (formerly minister of the Runcorn circuit). The anniversary proved highly successful and the collections reached the record krure of £3B.

In the morning the Rev. J. Hanby took as his text : " M4ster ! Where dwelleth thou," and said in his olin town on Thursday next they were going to comm-morate the invention of the powerloom by Cart- wright. On that day also they would celebrate the event of the relief of beleastured Mafeking. They were also keepinv up the Quoen'a birthday. I'Vhile,however,these events cluster round next Thursday they should not for- get that it was also the anniversary of the Ascension of Jesus Christ from this earth to begin his mediatorial work at the throne of God at the Father's right hand. One of the great features of the present day was the special prominence which had been given, and was being give,,,by the great teachers of e time to Jesus Christ liv- ing at that moment. There were truths of an obvious kind of a universally admi...ted character that did not grip them as they ought, Christian as well as ungodly persons were sometimes gospel hardened. It was a significant fact recorded in the life of the late Dr. bale, that it wa

in his latter ministry that he realised that Jesus Cnris was now living. He who died on Calvary, who was placed in the tomb and disappeared from the earth at his Ascension was living at that moment, If that wore true,as they affirmed it was,they were naturally anxious to know something about this Jesus. To know how Be

was spending His time and what He was doiag for His Church upon earth. For eeveral ye irs he, the preacher, had devoted himself to the stud c' of the events connected with the forty days. It would be well to regard these forty days, which ran thsir course next Thursday as typical dsys. They should be regarded as prophesying the whole of the ascended life of Jesus Christ in Heaven. They taught mueh concerning the body of Christ, concerning the present, His work, and His relationship to His disciples upon earth. " Master ! Where dwellest thou" became a question of great import, and as at the beginning of His ministry His contemporaries were anxious to know His dwelling place, they were not less anxious. He still dwelt with man and angels for Ho noticed that on the first day of the week when Mary came to the senulchre she noticed angels and the angels noticed her. He was also present with all mourners. The women watched all eight so that they might bring spices in the morning to embslm the body of Jesus. If death brought people near to Jesus it brought them back to Him. One of the groat lessens not learnt, so readily was that death was one of the great prerogatives to bring us back to Christ. He also dwelt beside the clinging and doubtful ones of his people. He had come to the conclusion that the weakest were the strongest and those who wore safest in his judgment, were after all in thr most perilous pesi- tion. He dwelt among those of his people who were engaged in daily tasks among his backsliders anci repentant noes. The most beautiful thin; recorded in the narrative was that Christ appeared unto Simon. Simon had cut himself away as John Wesley ssid as many members of society cut themselves away. They were not crosseJ off the book they were not thrust out of fellowship. It showed them how lovingly Jesus Christ renaired that relationship and brought it into evistenee again. Christ was only rep .rated from them by a c'otel. And since Pentecost that cloud even had disanneared. Many of them had proved this to be true. "Lo lam with you alway even to the end of the world." So whether they were mourners or whether they were lamenting the fact that life was dark and the struggle for existence made life monotonous or whether thee were clinging or doubting once they were sure in answer to the question "Where dwellest thou"? that he dwelt among them and that Christ had pledged hirnsslf to accompany them even to the end. Such he thought in brief was the the promise of these forty days. Occupying the pulpit again in the evening, the rev. gentleman founded an eloquent sermon full of life,enerey and truth, upon the words :—"lnstead of the fathers come thy children whom Thou meyest make princes in all the earth " Psalm 45-16. He spoke of the illustrious forefathers of Methodism, and particu- larly of the pioneers of Methodism in Runcorn, —Mr. Hezlehurst, Mr. Norman, Mr. Ravenscroft. and Mrs. Leadhetter. How well they all hail worked and how peacefully they all passel awas—and now their children were doing their work for God. They were occupying their places and carrying it on. He mede reference to the work of Mr. Ravenseroft as a Ossionar! in South Africa ; Mr. Charles Norman as a minister of the Gospel and Mr Collier, as an evangelist in the Manchester Mission. He forced home to the minds of his congregation the fact that they were connecting links between the past brilliant record and the great future and exhorted them to sec, to it that the work they did should be true and genuine, an that their children might look hack upon it with pleasure. In concluding, Mr. Hanby also made thrilling references to the war in South Africa.

A special feature of the anniversary was the excel- lency of the nausicil portion of the services. There were alyiut• 230 scholars and officers, sad these had ben well trained by Mr. Robert Yates. In addition, too, rho scholars were assisted by the Haltan-road Priz. choir The music included " Sans of Light." " Master sp air. thy servant heareth," "The Promiso of Life," " The Bread of Life," "Soldiers of the King," " Light at Eyenin2 Time." " Sons of Light" proved so effective that it was repeated by special tequest.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
Statement by Mr. Jenner Fust.

This Board met on Wednesday morning. Mr A J Jolley presided and there were also present :—Mrs Clay, Rev J H Riddette, Rev W II Drummonl, Dr Patterson, Messrs William Hickman, T H AglicToft. II Hibbert, J Billinge, H Forshaw, T B Melkin, 11 Thornton, A Brooks. T Halton, W Houv,liton, Clarke, A Jolley, G Pillin. J W Knowles, with Mr 3 C Sutton (clerk), Mr S Sutton (assist-ant clerk), Mr Ward (master), and Mr Wright (superintendent Pal gate Schools). Mr. Jenner Fast, Local Government Board In- spector, was likewise present. SCHOOLS COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of the above committee a letter from the Local Government Board having been read relating to the teachers' certificates, and the grants for the year ending La iy-day, 1901, and it app,arincy, that the system of reckoning the average atteniance waa'altered wi h the result thaf the a,sisl-ant scholmaster's grant was reduced from £45 to £37 125., it was recommended that the Clerk lay the matter before the Local Govern- ment Board and ask for an explanation,and at the same time endeavour to obtain the full grant carried by the asQistant schoolmaster's certificate. The minutes were approved, on the motion of the CHAIRMAN. seconded by MT. DAVIIS. HOUSE COMMITTEE—THE NEW CHAIRMAN,

Tha iminutes of the House Committee stated that Mr. William Hickman had been appointed chairman for the ensuing year, and the Rev. W. IT. Drummond vice- chairman. Reference was made in the minues to several appointments, and it was decided that the Master advertise for an assistant to the Matron and also for a laundress, each at the salary of £25 per annum, with uniform, rations, and apartments, The minutes were approved, the mover tieing Mr. HICKMAN, and the seconder the Rev. W DRUMMOND.

The Ctxnx read letters he had received on the sufijAct; of the emigration of children and the propnse:i extension of the period for the payment of building loans. As regarded banding loans, the Board had generally thought that 30 years wera graite long enough. (Hear, hear).
