div.p: THE REV J. J. LA.NGHAM.
Same correvondence from the Local Government Board with reference to the vacant chap'aincy waa read, and will be found in another column. ALTERATIONS AT THE WORKHOUSE.

The Clerk said he had received a latter that morning from th. Local Gevernment Board with reference to an amendA plan showing additions and alteratims at the Workhouse. The Board suggested certain alterations and asked that an amended plan be submitted together with an estimate of the cost. The communication was referred to the MUSA Com. mittee.
THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD AND MR. HOBSON.

A communication was read from the Local Govern- ment Board with reference to Mr. Benjamin Hobson's explanation respecting his work in the Great Sankey and Newton District, and informing. the Board that in the event of any future adverse reports they would consider the question of requiring his resignation. Mr. HOBSON was called into the room and acquainted with the decision of the Local Government Board. Mr. FORSHAV said that under the present system Mr. Hobson's district included Burtonwo d. The peope of that township complained that they hod to walk nearly six miles in order to register a death. Mr. KNOWLES stated that in the event of a change being made at any time he took it that the diitrict could be divided. The enainmAN said the Board would be very glad to meet the wishes of the residenti but they could not do anything at present. The question might be brought forward at some future time. SUGGESTIONS BY MR. JENNER FUST.

Mr. Jenner Fast stated that with reference to the last communication, the Board agreed with tIP alterations proposed with the exception of the bathrooms which were too small and the laundries, which he understood were being reconsidered,He thought the bathrooms could he made larger than at present shown without interfer- ing with the windows of the present building. Ha had recently had an opportunhy of making an inspoction of the wrrkhouse and he had one or two little things to mention but not of any great moment. In view of the opening of the new infirmary it wai not necessary for him to say anything about over-crowding for they were all hopinn, that that would be materially relieved hy!the new buildings. (Hear, hoar.) He should lihe to thank the Chairman for his kindness in inviting him to be present at the opening ceremony. Unfortun- ately he had to hold an inquiry at Whitehaven on that date which had been fixed for some time previously and be was therefore unable to be present. He wished them every success at the opening proceedings and every success for the new buildings which had boea put no with such great care and at considerable expense. (Heir, hear.) Mr. Jenne Fast then preceded to make suggestions of improvements at the workhouse including improvements to the female receiving wards and the sanitary arrangements. Be also considered it necessary that there should be better provision for fire 'escape at the projecting wings No 41 and 42 on the male side and 25 and 26 on the female side. He noticed that they had provided a kind of schute for the top storeys. He understood that there was a great objection to test its qualities—(laughter)—and if in ease of fire they bad to

exercise persuasion upon twenty or thirty women to go head foremost or feet foremost down the sehute he WO afraid the fire would have made considerable headway in the meantime. (Leugeter ) He was of opinion that schutee might be found convenient for children and able-bodied moo rather than sick people and old women. He would be glad if the Board :would consider the dealt ability of providing better means of fire escape where he had mentioned. No doubt the members of the Board had turned over in their minds the future of the old infirmary which was shortly to be vacated. The question was a difficult one and the difficulty was some- what increased by the fact that they were in a position of some doubt as to the future treatment of imbeeilee and epileptics. They had been expectieg legislation is the direction of removing these classes of patients frets! workhouses altogether: He was sorry to sea that the President of the Local Government Board announced the other day that as his plan would involve a demand nflog the Imperial Eechequer he did not see his war to propose legislation this year. That disposed of the qusstion rather indefinitely and it was a difficult thing to kaow what to advise He thought their old infirmary' would occupy an intermediate place between the work- house and the new infirmare and the Board might find it convenient to place there the old and infirm who were not in any need of actual nursing, but who were being taken care of and being made cornfortaele. The fieoll step necessary would te to employ someone to make 0 plan of the Ibuildinga as they are at present, and sutintl! a short report as to the condition of the walls, roofs awl the drains ; he must not forgot the drains because thef were out of sight. They would then be in a position tot, judge how far these buildings could be adopt" and bow far it Was desirable to retain tll, whole ef them. Turning to the schools he 13" made an inspection there and he thought the childreo were looking extremely well and doing very well, TO only drawback was a troublesome outbreak of ring w 002,, whnh was receiving attention and he hoped it Wont not spread much further. The CHAIRMAN : The children are now clear of it. Mr. JENNER FEIST (coetinuing) suggested that the children should be provided w!th lockers of their ovro 114 which they could store their own trifles. His attentloe was attracted by the amount of scrubbing which nis° necessary at the schools. Scrubbing was very desirahle but one could have too much of a good thing. It led t. dampness which was not wholesome for the childree• He thought if they could stain or varnish the floors the, might gst rid of a great deal of the scrubbing and tb6„ dermirories would be quite as healthy as they were au present.He would also like to direct attention to the desire" bitity of appointing a dentist- A great deal of suffering was caused to children by defective teeth and also injurf to their health by not being able to masticate their food properly. The practice was gaining grothad,particularll in the corteewestern district of having a dentist to par, occegional visits and examine the cbildren's teeth an do what was necessary As to payment he did 130 t tbiU they would find a very large payment necessary. might be arrang, d either by salary or by salary and fel per patient. Be hoped that next time he came he would, find them in full possession of their new infirmeeP (Hear, bear) The CHAIRMAN stated that most of the mattere which their attention bad been called had from time time exercised the midi of the House Committee at"' the Visiting Committee at Padgate. They had been eboi cussed several tim 'a in a more or less formal way, he conld assu, o the Inspector that they would receff• careful attention. The Rev. J. U. RIDDETTE said that with reference the last suggettien of the Insp ct.:(or, he noticed that number of men who 'seabed to enlist in the army as navy had been rejected on aceount of defective teetbo It was possible that some of tte,r boys would ultimate', find themselves in the navy or army, and be was 0,31:4 the Board would give a'tention te the suggestion be made with regard to the h ething ot the children. Them was another ale to the qof tion. Good teeth w.ere vett largely conducive to the enj ,yrnent of life. The Rasa they could do was to se that the children had soul, teeth with which to rneshcate the w hoessome food it which they were provided. (Laughter). Mr. FOESEI&W advocated the practice of using toot paste.

The CHAIRMAN said any rat-payer in the Union veal be allowed to witness the ceremony. This was all the business.

div.head: ACTION BY A WARRINGTCN THRASHING COMPANY.
div.p: ACTION BY A WARRINGTCN THRASHING COMPANY.
Pressing Hay for a Transport.

Before His Honour Judge Gwynne J3mes at the War- rington C:unty Couit last Thursday. a case was partly heard in which the Warrington and District Thrashing Company, of Bridge-foot claimed £45 12s for work done from Frederick Charles Ramsey ot Doe Park, Woolton, near Liverpool.—Mr. Browne represented the plaintiffs and Mr. Forshaw the defendant. Mr. Browne, in stating the plaintiffs' case, gave details of the account and explained how the various items were made out. The defendant contracted with the Govern- ment for the supply of hay for South Africa, and bought large quantities in the district surrounding Liver,ool. He asked the plaintiffs to press the hay for the trans- ports. They wore busy thrashing at the time and did not wish to leave their work in order to go to Gateacre and other plac:ls to press hay. The defendant was !n a hurry to get the hay on the transports and asked them to send the machines on at once. The plaintiffs replied that it would be impossible for them at the present time to undertake the work at 63 per ton of hay pressed which was the price they had previously charged. The defendant replied that the price was no object and that the work must be done without delay as one of the transports sailed in a few days. The plaintiffs were put toladditional expense in paying overtime and enzaging extra hands and pressed some hundreds of tons of hay at several places. The defendant was aware that the work was not being done under contract because he seat them a check for £3O after receiving a bill for ' the first lot of hay pressed. In answer to his Honour, Mr. Forshaw said the plain- tiffs had entered into a zontract!jto press the hay at 63. per ton. His Honour said he would hear evidence relating to the contract.

Walter Fitter, said he was one of the partners in the firm of the District Thrashing Company and remembered being rung up on the telephone on the 4th January. He answered the telephone and found that Mr. Ramsey was speaking, and be asked witness if they could press tome hay which was wanted immediately for a transport, Witness told him that they could not do the work at 6s. per ton as on a former occasion.Mr Ramsey said the price was no object and the work must be done immediately. They then sent the machines, although at the time they were busily engaged thrashing and pressing and had to stop that work in consequence. Mr Farrington was present is the office at the time and heard what witness said.

William Farrington, another partner in the firm, cor- rohorat ,d.—Cross-ex smined : He did not quote for any quintity at all in the telephonic message. Tile defendant gave evidence. Ho denied that the question of prico was mentioned by telephone before January 27ch.—Cross-cxamined : On the 14th January he sent the plaintiffs a cheque for £3O. Questioned by his H..inour : It was Mrs Ramsey's business, awl whatever he said through the telephone he said as her agent. His wife was not preaint in Court. Mr. Browne remarked that the claim was against M. Ramsey (male). 13-tenclant said that his name was Frederick Charles. His Honour said d efendant had sworn that if he did make any cmtract he did so as an agent for his wife. The consequence was that in suing M. Ramsey they had sued the right person but they had put the word male after the name instead of female. He (his Honour) would allow them to amend the claim He should see that whatever the rights of the case were Ithat justice was done. He wanted to save expense as much as he could but at the same time to go into the merits and rights of the case and for that purpose he should adjourn the case, in the meantime he would amend the claim by substituting the words F C Ramsey for M Ramsey and give plaintiffs leave to add Marion Graham Ramsey. This case will be heard on June 14th.

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS.
The Advance on the Vaal.
Lord Roberts on the Rhenoster. Official Despatch.

The War Office, yesterday morning, issued the following despatch fram Lord Roberta to the Secre- tary of State for War : South Bank, Rhenoater River, 1.30 p.m., May 23. We found on our arrival here this morning that tke enemy had fled during the night.

They had occupied a strong position on the north bank of the river, which had been carefully in- trenched, but they did not think it advisable to .defend it, when they heard that lan Hamilton's force was at Heilbron, and our cavalry, which crossed the Rhenoster some miles lower down the stream, was threatening the right rear. The bridge over the Rhenoster, several culverts, and some miles of the railway have been destroyed. lan Hamilton's troops drove the Boers, under Piet De Wet, before thed from Lindley to Heilbren. The passage of the Rhenoster was stoutly dis- puted, and our loss might have been heavy, but for a well concerted plan which brought Smith_ Dorrien's brigade on to the enemy's flank just at the right moment.
The offiser commanding at Boshof reports that upwards of 350 Free Staters have surrendered dur- ing the last few days, who have given up 360 rifles, about one hundred horses, and a large amount of
ammunition.
Boer Account of the Ambuscade. Eight Killed, Thirteen Wounded.
BOER CAMP, VOLKERUST, MAY 20.

Late yesterday afternson the Boer outposts at- tacked a body of English troops between Nqutu and Mount Prospect, two peaks south of biajuba. Eight of the British were killed and thirteen wounded. Thera were no casualties on the Boer side, but three horses were killed. The burghers are more deter- mined than ever to resist the invasion of the Trans- vaal. To-day everything is quiet. British Patrols in the Transvaal.
A telegram from Newcastle states that our patrols have crossed the Buffalo River and entared Trans- vaal territory unopposed.

div.head: EVENTS OF THE WEEK. THE RELIEF OF MAFEKING. Despatch from Baden-Powell. SMART FIGHTING.

HONINGB SPRWIT, 221,1 P MAY, _3.45 P.M.

Northern and southern columns joined hands on 15th. Attacked enemy yesterday (lAsh), and after smart engagement entirely defeated them with loss. British casualties, three killed, 22 wounded.
Relieving force marched into itafeking this morning

div.head: With the Warrington Volunteers.
div.p: With the Warrington Volunteers.

The following has been received by Mr %V. Potimore, hairdresser, of Golborne-street, from Sergeant P. Ro-k a Warrington Volunteer in Natal :—Elandslaagfe, April 25t11.—We landed at Capetown on the 17c.h larch and went into camp for three day 3, and it was a camp, nothing but dry bread and sand to eat Capetown bself is all right. If it were not for seeing niggera one could not tall the difference from a town at home. We were six days getting to Durban. We were quartered at Durban for three days. owing to fever breaking out. suppose you heard of Private Blackwood's death. Poor chap ! He was taken ill the second day on bpard the Guelph. and when we left him at Durban it veined to break him up altogether. He died en the 2nd of April from pleurisy. We took train at Durban for Ladysmith, 14 heurs' ride; travelling all night.we got to badysinith at six next morning. The first thing we saw was the River !Clip fell of sand bags, by which the Boers had tried to flood the town, hut it didn't "come off." When we got to the regiment they were camping three miles out of the town on Surprise Hill, where the Boers had one of their Long Toms. We stayed there for a week and then went on to march for twelve mites to Modder Spruit one day, and the next six miles to Elandelaagte, where the Boers were reported to be massing in large numbers. We are close to the Biggarsberg Mountains, where we expect they will either give in or fight jolly hard to get out, as we have them surrounded on all aides. Our artillery now and again gives them a taste of lyddite. Our regiment is escort to the naval guns, one of the worst jobs there is. We have to be with them night and dayjand we are lucky if we get three nights in bed out of seven. There is not much to see here, ex- cept hills and camps. If we want a bottle of ginger beer we have to pay 9d. for it.

div.head: Warrington Ambulance Men.
div.p: The Warrington Ambulance Men.

Private W. E. Longinore, of the 24th Field Hospital Field Forces, South Africa, writing on April 24th to Captain Waring,Chief Superintendent of the Warrington Branch of the St. John Ambulance Association, states that he and his comrades are now as far as Kimberley, having left De Aar OR the 22nd of April. He continues. —To-morrow we go to Dronfield, following up the 10th Division (sixth brigade),so we are very near to the front. The object of our leader is to go to Mafeking and then Pretoria. I think we axe the first men of the St. John Ambela.nee Brigade to get so far up country. While we /were at De Aar, Holloway . and Newnes passed through •!--1 their way to Bloemfontein. They will probably meet di at Pretoria. We were all very pleased to bear of our three officers—Mr. Crosfield and Williams and Mansuer —being accepted. Our officers are very kind to us. • . We are all in good health and send our best wishes. On our way up we passed the places where Lord Methuen fought the battles of Belmont, Graspan, Molder River and Magersfontein, and are now camped in sight of where General French relieved Kimberley.

div.head: Warrington Policeman with
div.p: A Warrington Policeman with
General Roberts.

The following is au extract from a lett 3.7 received by P.C. Howard. from P.C. J. W. Hurst. a Warrington policeman in the 3rd Grenadier Guards, who is with Lord Roberts :—Bloemfontein, April 28th. lam pleased te tell you we are happy now that we know we are getting the best of the Boers, and if we have good luck i we shall soon he n Pretoria. Then it will not be long before we shall return home. lam working in Bloem- fontein !on a railway ,engine, and have been doing so since sie took Bloemfontein. I was the firat driver to take a train out of Bloemfontein when I took half a battalion of Grenadiers to see if the line was all right al far as Orange River, where general Gstacre's division was fighting. The line was clear and no Beers abou t. We, therefore, could use the line from Capetown to Bloemfontein, a ditance of 750 miles. The Boers Wee: up the Orange River bridge, but we soon bad another one trade. Now the troops will not suffer so much by marching to this place, and they have the railway behind them all the way to Pretoria. Our last two marches were 40 miles, and we did it in 24 hours. for which Lord Roberta gave ua great prai,e. l'he people talk atout the Guards in times of psace,but I find thee have to do what others cannot do in times of war. We have been he all the battle out here before and since Lord Roberta came out.

div.head: Private J. Burton's Experiences. "Fly Soup."
div.p: Private J. Burton's Experiences. "Fly Soup."

Mi. Burton, Hatton Vida, Grappenhall-road,Stockton Heath, has r( c 4ived a letter from her brother Private J. Burton of the 4th Kings Own Royal Lancaster Regiment In it the writer says :—" We landed at Capetown and went te De Aar And from there to Naauwpoort. We were there for two months and we had a lively time of it, sleeping out at night in the trenches and getting
RELIEF OF MAFEKING,

Loud swell the strain of Britain's voice, As old and young, in song rej3ice ; And far-off lands who wish it well, In unison the chorus swell! "God save the Queen "—the people pray'd, The God of battles came to aid, And in that shout of victory, Powell and Maleltio,g are free! Chorus—Hurrah ! hurrah, for victory Hurrah ! three times for victory ! For while we sing of Mafeking, We sing in praise for victory. Bravely, as heroes bold they stand, That nobly half-fed little band; Within grim walls, as prisoners bound ; While thousands of the foe surround! Yet once, again, old country dear, Thy sons united, staad nor tear; The Empire's universal breath Is fight for honour, or for death !" Chorus.—Hurrah! hurrah for victory So. JAMES MUIR.

div.head: BADEN-POWELL.
div.p: BADEN-POWELL.
Hero of Mafeking. Odr li:mpire's Gideon thou, liler history shall wreath thy brow. Before thy might her foemen reeled Faithful! Well done! Thy record sealed.
Honour the brave and bold! Joy! With a joy untold. Lift up your hearts and pray, Thank God for this glad day; And cheer—with a mighty ring— The Hero of Mafeking !

Relief of Mafeking, Hurrah! Hurrah ! At last it's here: "Relief of Mafeking" ! we hear. Quickly, the message flashed along, Filling the Empire's heart with song: Changing its beat, from silent flow, To quicker pulse and brighter glow. Siren, and foghorn, loudly swell, Screeching and thrilling first to tell. The crowd around they soon incite With ecstacies of keen •:elight. A million banners wave on high, Their gorgeous folds towards the sky; Bells, from a million turrents, sound • Their joyous paeon all around; Trumpet, and harp, and sound of drum, Join in the glad encomium ; Lights, from a million torches, blaze O'er the glad land to join the praise Joy in a million hearts uprise ! A million voices reach the skies. Our Boys and Girls, a joyous band, For brave "8.P." their lungs expand. Tin whistles ! Squeakers ! charmed we view, Which,erstwhile, would our courage screw. No sound, discordant, can be found, For "8.P." mellows all around. And, babas in arms, with wondering eyes, Spring to the jpy which satisfies. A "Colour' they must carry too To join the Powell grand review. Or Empire's Sons—Colonial Bred,— Gather with joy her fame to spread; Gladly they joined the battle's din Their Motherland's just wars to win. As one! Victoria's sons stand firm ! And alien foes contempted spurn. They rally round their Mother Queen, With reverent love and joyful mien. In phalanx firm, they face the foe. Solid, they strike and overthrow! Red, White, and Blue, solidity! The "Union Jack "and Victory! Where'er it waves its rule shall be: "God and the Right and Liberty." And ages yet unborn ehall sing TILE BRAVE DEFENCE OF MAFEKING ! " DEWI BEIM."

div.head: WITH APOLOGIES TO MR. ALFRED
div.p: WITH APOLOGIES TO MR. ALFRED
AUSTIN.

HERE'S a vexatious thing, " Relief of Mafeking." Now must the Llureate sing, Sing for the many. Poorly the rapture climbs, Yet must I send some rhymes Fit for to-morrow's "Times," From Abergavenny. Kimberley, Ladysmith— What must I rhyme it with? Strange from its wedded" kith" " Kin " thus to sever : Here's a confounded name, Hard in a verse to frame. " Baden" must lack his fame, `• Powell " for ever! Rhymes are galore with" year," " Near " I've used twice, I fear, Perhaps they may kick at" spear," 'Cos they don% use 'em : Making "fierce cannon leap" Is perhaps a little steep, Hope they will think it deep, Fear ' twill confuse 'em. Confound this wretched verso So plaguey hard and terse: Just makes a poet curse Working for hours : Bother old Drayton's shade, Bother the verse he made, Bother " The Light Brigade," Now for my flowers.
" Daily News."

div.head: MILITARY NOTES.
div.p: MILITARY NOTES.

1 Several non-commissioned officers and men ot the local forces in Natal who distinguished themselves in the recent operations conducted by Sir Redvers Buller which led to the relief of Ladysmith and who were recommended for commissions in the regular army have now been appointed to Second Lieuten- ancies. Trooper Travis Cook, of the Natal Mounted Police, has been gazetted Second Lieutenant in the South Lancashire Regiment joining the Ist battalion now in South Africa. Sub-Inspector Fynney, an officer of the Natal Mounted Police, who specially distinguished himself and Sergeant Dinnen, South African Light Horse together with Trooper Neville Field, Natal Mounted Rifles, have been appointed Second Lieutenants in the Liverpool Regiment, all three joining. the Ist battalion of the regiment now in South Afr;ca. Lieutenant Lang•lon has been promoted to the rank of Captain in the Liverpool Regiment. He joined the sth Battalion Liverpool Regiment at Warrington in Oetober 1891 and in 1893 got hie commission in the regular service when he was appointed Second Lieutenant in the let battalion Liverpool Regiment. As Captain Langdon is at present away from the regiment serving with the Egyptian Army, Lieutenant Hawthorn has been promoted Captain in the Liverpool Regiment and he joined the corps in March 1894. Captain Ferrets late of the 2ad battalion South Lancashire Regiment, has been appointed to com- mand a company in the Royal Lancashire Reserve Regiment. Captain Ferrets joined the South Lan- cashire Regiment from the militia in December 1883; became Captain in 1893; retired a few years ago and was then appointed Captain, reserve of officers. Second-Lieutenant Dickson of the 2nd Volunteer Battalion Cheshire Regiment, has been given a commission in the regular army becoming Second- Lieutenant in the Cheshire Regiment. He joined

div.head: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL. " THE-ELSI3GET."
div.p: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL. " THE-ELSI3GET."

An extraordinary meeting of the Urban District Council for the purpose of levying the rates for 1900-1901 was held in the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Monday afternoon. Mr. W. Collingwood presided and there were also present, Mes,rs. C B F Borron, J W Emmett, Siddeley, Gilmour, W od, Sitnostn, Dr Patterson, Ormand, Evans, Thomp‘on and W W Shirley (clerk). THE RELIEF OF MAFEICING.

The Chairman said that before proceeding with the business of the Council. he fel; some reference should be II made to the extraordinary feeling throughout ties country in regard to the relief of Mafeking. (Hear, hear) I As representatives of that township they must all feel heartily thankful to the Almighty first of all and second:yr to the instruments used by him, the soldiers I and brave representatives of the army wh3 had held out so nobly in their resistance all these months—far the I splendid relief which had taken piece. (Hear. hear). "THE BUDGET "—NO INCREASE IN THE RITES. Mr, Ormand,the Chairman of the Finance Committee, said that before formally moving the resolution relative to the rates for the ensuing year, he supposed they would expect some little statement from him as to what had lean done during the year ending 31st of March last,and also as to what was prop -sed to be done during the year ending March 315t,1901.1t was a very pleasing duty in the fact that they did not propose to iecrease the rat's in the aggregate this year, and the reasons he thought would prove to them to be obvious. The General Improvement fund account during the year. eroding March 31st showed an income of £3946 and an expenditure of £4,053, givine an excess of expenditure over income of £lO7. They estimated 12 months agn a surplus of £254 which with the defi- ciency of £lO7 left £361 to be accounted for. New Line of Steamers to Douglas.

A new service between Liverpool and Oouglas is to be commenced next Saturday (June 2nd). Two beautiful fast paddle steamers with electric light installation, named the "Lily" and "Ireland" have been purchased by the Liverpool and Douglas Steamers, Ltd , and one of them will sail from the Prince's Stage at 11-30 a.m. on the day named, re- turning from Douglas at -30 p.m. A second steamer will leave the Prince's Stage for Douglas at 1 p.m. the samo day and there will also be sailings on Bank Holiday. The return second class fare is 3s Gc.l and first class 5s GI. There is every promise of a large number availing themselves of these cheap sailings during the Whitsuntide holidays. 1

div.head: RELIEF OF MAFEKING• --- • • Saturday's Rejoicings at Warrington.
div.p: THE RELIEF OF MAFEKING• --- • • Saturday's Rejoicings at Warrington.

The streets of Warrington presented a gay and festive appearance on Saturday when the rejoicings attendant upon the reception of the news of the re- lief of Mafeking were continued. From every build- ing floated the National flags and streamers spanned almost every thoroughfare. On the flag staff at the Town Hall a Union Jack bearing the words " Mafe- king "and " 8.P." had been hoisted with streamers on either side. The flags in some eases were ern- bsllished with pvrtraits of the gallant defender of Mefeking and patriotic mottoes. Effigies of Oom Paul were to be seen in several quarters of the town, and in many instances were excellent " make-ups." In one streets Mr. and Mrs. Kruger;were sitting at a table on which were glasses of beer, and effigies suspended by the'neck were the cause of much amusement. The day was observed as a general holiday most of the works closing in the morning and the street were thronged with people. Every- one sported patriotic emblems, and medallions bear- ing Baden-Powell's photo were greatly en evidence. The children kept the day in a manner worthy of the occasion. Boys and girls paraded the town dressed in a variety of costumes. Some played the rale of "Red Cross Knights " and opportunity was taken of soliciting contributions to the Indian famine and war funds. Everyone was in the best of humours and there were general ex- preQsions of admiration of the manner in which the little Mafekiug garrison had undergone such priva- tions and kept the enemy at bay. During the day the band of Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co. paraded the streets followed by the large banner of the Bed- stead Makers Society. In the evening lively scenes were witnessed. From the roof of the Town Hall coloured lights were displayed and explosives dis- charged. The streets were again crowded until a late hour.

The rejoieings over the relief of the'Mafeking Garrison were continued on Monday evening and have been kept up with more or less enthusiasm throughout the week. A torchlight procession was organised on Monday evening and headed by the band from Messrs Crosfieid'e Works paraded the thoroughfares of the town. This celebration was in honour of Baden-Powell's promotion and that gallant officer's portrait was a prominent feature in the procession. The processionists decked themselves out with red, white and blue favours and the Union Jack. The younger element provided themselves with a band on their own account corno.,sed of whistles and rsttles and tin biscuit boxes (the latter for drums). They para ied the s reets to thnir discordant music, singing patriotic songs and other popular ditties.

div.head: Thanksgiving Service at Wycliffe Church. Sermon by the Rev. J. Yonge.
div.p: Thanksgiving Service at Wycliffe Church. Sermon by the Rev. J. Yonge.

IA thanksgiving service for the relief of Mafeking was held at Wycliffe Church on Sunday morning. There was a good c eigregation and special music was rendered in- cluding the" Te Deum " and the" Hallelujah Chorus." The Rev. John Yonge preached an appropriate dis- course from the words "Songs of Deliverance" Psalm xxx.i. 7. He said it was to songs and shouts and rejoic- ines of that kind that all classes of people from the palace to the cottage since Friday night had been com- pletely given up. They began, iedeed, on Wednesday last at besieged Mafeking itself at the instant that the long looked-for relief column came in sight. Subsequently they had broken forth, in swelling volume wherever the tidings had gone. The whole Empire, in all parts of fire world, for long past had its gaze fixed upon the little South African town which, during seven weary, but patient and heroic months had been so closely and hotly besieged. Since the relief of Ladysmith and Kimberley from similar beleagurements, Mafeking had absorbed the universal thought, and held the whole Empire in an intense strain of anxious suspense. And now that the relief hal been effected, the long pent up feelings of British hearts every- where had found varied, but harmonious expression, in "Songs cf Deliverance." However men might differ in opinibn about the war itself all were united in the j )y of that deliverance. Every city and village and home and heart throughout the Dominions of the Queen,—men women and chiliren—were throbbing with the same feelings of relief, gratification, gratitude and triumph. Indeed it might be truly said ,hat the thrill of delight had pulsated round the globe. Rarely had the swiftness of the telegraph received more splendid illustration or produced more electric effect. Hitherto, c netinental nations had been severe in their criticisms of the British people for embarking in this war. They had said many hard things, and it had seemed as if no nation could be more unpopular abroad than our own. But the news of the relief of Mafeking had not only in- terested but in measure, placated our critics. It appeared that even our most hostile critics had be looking on with admiration of the defenders of little Mafeking and its relief -was extorting from the most unwilling of them a sympathetic cheer. Indeed it a!rnost looked as if our very enemies., the Beers themselves, did not seriously begrudge that victory. This defence had been so gallant, so resolute, so resourceful, so self sacrificingly devoted, that the very Beers had been the first to let us know of the suc- cess. The incident reminded them of Mecaulay's well- known lines in his " Lays of ancient Rome," when he ' described, how, when Horatius, having hewn down the bridge which else had given admission ta 1131113 to the armies of the advancing Tuscans, plunged headlong into the waters of the Tiber amid the bewildered sileace alike of friend and foe—and how all stood gazing where he sank, and when his crest appeared above the waters All Rome sent forth a rapturous cry— And even the ranks of Tocany Could scarce forbear to cheer I It was human nature to admire courage, hardihood, endurance, patience in suffering, psrsistence in endeavour, indomitable, unconquerable fortitude. And such was the admiration without reserve or stint, which Baden Powell, with his brave force, and the British and native people of Mafeking, had merited and were now receiving from the whole world. Coming so immedi- ately close to Sunday as that glad news had done, it was simply impossible to abstain from referring to it. Nor could there be any reason why they should abstain. Indeed there was every reason why they should not. When in the early stages of this terrible war, our armies met with reverses and disasters when their ears were con- tinually assailed by "evil tidings," their hearts were bewildered and distressed, they turned for relief and help to the teaching of that sacred Book. They then learned how the true believer in God was spoken of as one who was " not afraid of evil tidings because his heart is fixed trusting in the Lord." There was at that time, a very considerable turning Godward, in this nation and the reckless, arrogant, self confidence which had sent off the troops amid only too many scenes of bravado and revelry was exchanged for more sober and serious methods, and they were sent off amid prayer as well as plaudits. Surely, now, then in this brighter day when God seemed to be responding to the prayers of British hearts—and when the relief of Mafeking and the successes of the recent weeks, appeared to promise a speedy ending of the war—they might well remember God. In His house, on His day, they might well" Bless His holy name" for national mercies and remember Him as their giver. It was Be who "caused us to triumph " and"cempasseth us about with conga of deliverance." After referring to his text the rev, gentleman said he ventured to say that anyone might learn a good deal from the tenacity, the uncon- querable persistence of the commander of Mafeking. They should do what Sir George White did at Lady- smith, Colonel Kekewich, at Kimberley, and Baden- Powell at Mafeking. They must '• sit-tight" and never Five in. It seemed to him that these brave defenders of the beleegured South African towns had been preaching a very strong and much needed gospel to men of this sadly enervated genera- tion. How often did they find men weakly succumbioe before life's temptations, yielding to the forces of circumstances sacrificing itheir very manhood to the desire for any easy course and justifying their surrender by the plea that circumstances had been too many for them: There was a tremendous amount of moral cowardice and poltroonery in ordinary life. In conclusion the preacher said he thought they could understand something of the surpassing emotions that muat have filled the hearts of both relievers and relieved at Ladysmith, Kimberley and last Wednesday at Male- king. There were not only shouts of exultation but tears of joy. Even the least martially disposed among us, he thought could like to have shared in the sublime, never to be foreotten experience and sensation and he couressed that he had envied the proud pleasure of the prompt and enterprising London pressman in whose office first the telegraphic tape began to spell out the news of the relief, who instantly dashed off express to tell the mother and sister of Baden Powell that the deliverance had come. " Songs of De- liverance" indeed, nothing less, nothing other would suffice. Songs of deliverance mingled with tears of joy- What they had to remeenber,and what they hoped would be remembered, more or less by all our nation was this, that the real author and giver of all songs of deliverance was Ged. They must not oherish the idea that the cour- age that had sustained the brave defenders at Mafeking eaabling them to hold on and held out these seven weary menths, or the energy, enterprise or valour that enabled the relieving column to rescue the beleagnred town had been simply the exhibition of racial, natural qualities and the result of Beitish skill, patience and pluck. Granting that these qualities had in- strumentally resulted in the deliverance, let it not be* forgotten from whom they had been derived. Neither let it be forgotten that there had been a watchful, careful Providence over-ruling the interests of that endangered people. From multitudes of hearts in this nation many prayers had gone up for the success of our arms, for the success of lour endangered

garrisons, and for tke speedy ending of a strife which was lamentable even though it might be just, and therefore in the achievement oi this deliver- ance, songs of gratitude should be offered unto the Lord. As regarded Mafeking, at any rate, even such as had disapproved the war could have no difficulty in thanking God for that deliverance. And if that, along with the other successes of the latter days, brought lot, near and early prospect the termination of the painful, terrible strife—and the establishment of permanent and honourable and equitable peace—still more should they be bound to give thankful praises unto God. These were days for something more and deeper than emotions of pride in victory or joy in longed for deliverances, they were days for songs of thankfulness to Almighty God.

div.head: Latchford.
div.p: Latchford.

The children of Christ Church Parish, Latchford, cele- brated the news of the relief on Saturday evening by walking in procession through the village and making a collection for the fund for providing a trip to the sot for the Mafeking women and children, as suggested by General Baden-Powell. They collected 2135. 61., which has been forwarded to Miss Broadbent for the object named. The people of Latchford generally received the welcome news of the relief with much enthusiasm.

div.head: Lymm.
div.p: Lymm.

The news of the relief of Mafeking was received at the Lymm Telephone Exchange a few minutes after 9.30 on Friday night and cannons were soon being let off and fireworks were to be seen all over the village. At the Conservative Club the president proposed the health of the Queen, the British Forces in South Africa, and the gallant Baden-Powell,and the members sang the National Anthem and gave cheers for all concerned. In addition to the fireworks at the Club, a gentleman across the road blazed away from a bedroom widow with a revolver, the crowd greatly appreciating his efforts to add to the din. In the village tin cans, trays, handbells, a hurdy-gurdy, and " all kinds of music" were quickly commandeered, and what were considered to be respect- able and sober-minded citizens were capering all over the place and dancing to the strains of a barrel-organ. On Saturday night there was a large crowd in the village, and the tradesmen met and decided to have a further display of fireworks, and for several hours a band played the National Anthem and a number of patriotic airs.

div.head: Winwick.
div.p: Winwick.

In this parifik the news was received about ten o'clock by telegram at the Post Office, ke., when the bells of the Parish Church were rang and much enthusiasm pre- vailed. Patriotic songs were sung, and Saturday seas observed as a general holiday.

div.head: Stockton Heath.
div.p: Stockton Heath.

Stockton Heath, in common with otksr places, was in a state of rejoicing over the relief of Mafeking. The vil- lage was gaily decorated and children filled with patri- otic spirit paraded the streets singing "Soldiers of the Queen" and other appropriate airs.

div.head: Accident at Widnes.
div.p: Accident at Widnes.

During the rejoicings at Widnes for the relief of Male- king on Friday night, Mr: Thomas Daintith, son of the late Mr. Thomas Daintith, of the Rams Head Inn, G:apponhall, residing at Oakland-street, Widnes, had the misfortune to he knocked down in the crush and have his leg brokea. Mr. Daiatith, who is an engine driver, was takea to the Accident Hospital, where the injured limb was sat, and we are pleased to state that be is progressing favourably.

div.head: Jubilations at Earlestown.
div.p: Jubilations at Earlestown.

To say that the district of Earlestown and Newten was jubilant on the receipt of intelligence that the sorely beseiged little town of Mafeking,had been relieved, is to put the case very mildly indeed. Such scenes of enthusi- asm have not been witnessed by"the oldest inhabitant." About 945 on Friday night which by the way was market night when many people were busily engaged purchasing their supplies they were electrified by the anxiously expected news that Meddling was relieved. The first to receive the information was Mr. Thomas Molyneux of Market-street,and within a very brief space the buzzer at Messrs. Sloe and Co.'s works was sounding the joyful news to all and sundry. The cue was taken up and very soon pandemonium reigned, buz- zers and bells helping to make night hideous. Business became a thing ef the past and it was wonder- ful to see the magical effect the intelligence had upon the people. Men and women were running here and there hurrahing to the top of their bent, and flags and streamers were goon flying in all directions. Market- street quickly became filled with a surging mass of people. and Mr. Melyneux illuminated the front of his shop with variegated lights. Unfortunately, however, when the illuminations were in full blaze a large sign gave way and craehed down on the lanterns, putting them out of the rejoicings for good. Luckily the people were gathered in the roadway, and owing to this no- body was injured. Quickly the tradespeople put up I their shutters and the town was given over to the people whose boisterousness was uncontrolled by the police. A monstro procession was organised, and soon a vast crowd of people were cheering, to the full extent of their lungs, the patriotic songs "Soldiers of the Queen," " Lively little lads in Navy blue " and " God save the Queen," came in for a lot of attention, whilst on every hand could be heard the expressions " Good old Baden-Powell," " New for Pretoria," " Where's old Kruger " and so on. The juvenile male portion had by some means become , possessed of innumerable crackers, and these they set off indiscriminately much to the terror of the ladieg. In the impromptu precession,was a large wooden model of a 4.7 gun drawn on a carriage and lettered " Bul!er's Pet,' and on a pony was an effigy of Kruger. Rockets were plentifully dispersed and until three o'clock in the morning the streets were a lively appearance. At the Vulcan Foundry a large number of men were on night duty, but as soon as they learnt the news they ceased operations and joined the shouting throng. At Newton, the enthusiasm and rejoicing was f q tally as hilarious as at Earlestown, and a procession beaced by the Volunteer bugle band gave vent to their exabtrance. On Saturday the buzzers of several works sounded but it was only at the Viaduct Werke that a number of men turned up, and it was evident they only put in an appearance to get nessession of t'no implements of war- fare which they bad made and hidden in anticipation of the event. Certainly there was no intention of settling

down to work, for at the early hour of half•past six, several hundred men and lads formed in procession and marched down to the residence of the superintendent of the works. Mr. J. W. Emmett and serenaded him by singing patriotic songs. They afterwards left the works and did not again put in an appearance. At about 10 o'clock, thousands of people made their way to the raarket ground,where a gigantic procession was formed. The Viaduct Works Band was at the head, and on horse- back was Mr. te. Owen, a Crimean veteran. Banners were innumerable, and humorous mottoes were in evidence such as" Good old Baden," What price cld Kruger now." Many of the men were armed with anti- quated rifles, and a very large number carried swords, and other fearsome implements. Many were dressed in khaki, and several effigies were carrtecl. An amusing one was Kruger suspended by the neck from a gallows, whilst another showed the old gentleman safely secured in a net, whilst Steyn was also in safe keeping. The procession was unique in its way, and paraded the whole district by way of Wargrave and Newton, the effigies being finally burnt on the Market Square. At night there was again a big muster and a torchlight procession was organised and held, but it suffered greatly in comparison with the morning pro- ' cession. Several of the tradespeople had come down handsomely with subseriptions for the provision ef fire- works, and a collection was made during the progress ot the procession in aid of the Indian Famine Fund. It was after nine o'clock before the procession got fairly under weigh and it was nearly 11 o'clock when it returned to the Market Ground. There was a fair dis- play of fireworks, and it was past midnieht before the streets were cleared. Mr. Molyneux interested himself very much in the proceedings and through his generosity over £4 were handed in for the fund. Ou Sunday after- now: a thanksgiving service was conducted on the Markct Square by the Rev. T. R. Matthews, and refer- ences were made in most of the places of worship, the National Anthem being sung.

div.head: How Run corn Rejoiced.
div.p: How Run corn Rejoiced.

The good news of the relief of Mafeking was first annohneed to the Runcorn public by our enterprising bwn'sman, Mr. D. H. Jones (of Messrs. Jones and Sons) High-street, whose windows have been for some weeks past filled with interestin war items and cartoons. A large flag, with "Relief of Mafeking" in red letters upon a white ground.and edged with sweet toned toy bells was run out of the principal window. Shortly afterwards the announcement was received at the General Post Office, and by Mr. Mack, Savages Bridge, who also has been prominent as a kind of "deputy war offiee." Immedi ately the crowd felt sure of it, the fun commenced, and the streets were soon thronged. Large crowds of young men solved the difficulty of blowing tin whistles, cornets, bugles, and sarryin: two or three flags or torches at the same time. Bonfires and fireworks were lighted and everything done that could be to show appreciation, and give vent to the rent-up feelings of joy following days of anxiety. Although, all were per- vaded with the spirit of a burlesque, the large crowd were thrilled with a deep sense of thankfulness for the relief of the gallant garrison. On Saturday the event was, further kept up,and many were the effigils of " Poor Kruger" that were carried around in triumph by the juveniles. Some, emabined their amusement with the sensibleness of collecting funds for the relief of our soldiers and sailors' depend- ents and the local funds were swelled not a little as a result.
Oa Sunday, there were no special memorial services, but almost all ministers reminded their congregations of the debt they owed to the Almighty for His mercifulness and giacicusness.

div.head: " RIOT " AT WESTON. Constable Assaulted.
div.p: A " RIOT " AT WESTON. Constable Assaulted.

Before Messrs. F. J. Norman and W. Handley, at Run- corn Petty Sessions on Monday John ID'grata's, of Riley's Court, Weston, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and assaulting P.C. Wylie while in the execution of his duty.—P.o Wylie stated that at 7-30 p.m. on Saturday, he was at home when he received information that the prisoner was misconducting him- self. He went out and found the prisoner in Heath-road, minus coat and hat, and behaving in a most disorderly manner. His language was not fit for a human being to hear. Witness requested him to '.o home but he refused to go for a--like him, and he got hold of him and led him to hits house and asked him to go inside. The prisoner instead of doing so attacked him and kicked him in shameful fashion. He was obliged to defend himself and he put the prisoner down five times. While they were struggling together prisoner's father and mother and several other persons came up. The mother picked up witness's cane and thrashed him severely over the legs and back. The father at the same time also illused him. It. was a regular riot. After a great struggle he brought the prisoner to Runcorn. The prisoner was very'drunk.Witness had more trouble with the prisoner's family than the whole village of Weaton.—Deective Sergeant Gregory testified to the prisoner's drunken aonditien at the Police Station. The prisoner alleged ,-hat he was " fresh " but not drunk and accused the officer of having struck him. He called Mary Austin, a neighbour, who said she did see the prisoner with his father and mother, strike the constable but she had not see the whole bother. Superintendent Pearson put in the prisoner's record, and said a policeman ha a rural district was alone and he had enough to do without struggling with a great big fellow like the prisoner. The constable had given the prisoner every chance and the prisoner ought to be dealt with severely,—Mr. Norman said the prisoner's record was a very bad one. He got drunk and then did not know what mischief he did. The magistrates must defend the constables from this sort cf thing. Per being drunk the prisoner was fined ss. and costs. Ss or seven days, and for the assault he was fined 40; and cost Bs, or 21 days hard labour; the sen tences to run concurrently.
